paragraphs.text: "Then spake Jesus to the multitudes and to His disciples, saying, The Scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: all therefore whatsoever they bid you do, that do; but do not after their works."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: Then. When? When He had said these things, when He had stopped their mouths; when He had brought them that they should no more dare to tempt Him; when He had shown their state incurable.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: And since He had made mention of "the Lord" and "my Lord," He recurs again to the law. And yet the law said nothing of this kind, but, "The Lord thy God is one Lord." But Scripture calls the whole Old Testament the law.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But these things He saith, showing by all thinks His full agreement with Him that begat Him. For if He were opposed, He would have said the opposite about the law; but now He commands so great reverence to be shown towards it, that, even when they that teach it are depraved, He charges them to hold to it. But here He is discoursing about their life and morals, since this was chiefly the cause of their unbelief, their depraved life, and the love of glory. To amend therefore His hearers; that which in the first place most contributes to salvation, not to despise our teachers, neither to rise up against our priests, this doth He command with superabundant earnestness.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But He does not only command it, but also Himself doth it. For though they were depraved, He doth not depose them from their dignity; to them rendering their condemnation heavier, and to His disciples leaving no cloke for disobedience.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: I mean, that lest any one should say, that because my teacher is bad, therefore am I become more remiss, He takes away even this pretext. So much at any rate did He establish their authority, although they were wicked men, as even after so heavy an accusation to say, "All whatsoever they command you to do, do." For they speak not their own words, but God's, what He appointed for laws by Moses. And mark how much honor He showed towards Moses, again showing His agreement with the Old Testament; since indeed even by this doth He make them objects of reverence. "For they sit," He saith, "on Moses' seat." For because He was not able to make them out worthy of credit by their life, He doth it from the grounds that were open to Him, from their seat, and their succession from him. But when thou hearest all, do not understand all the law, as, for instance, the ordinances about meats, those about sacrifices, and the like for how was He to say so of these things, which He had taken away beforehand? but He meant all things that correct the moral principle, and amend the disposition, and agree with the laws of the New Testament, and suffer them not any more to be under the yoke of the law.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: Wherefore then doth He give these things divine authority, not from the law of grace, but from Moses? Because it was not yet time, before the crucifixion, for these things to be plainly declared.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But to me He seems, in addition to what has been said, to be providing for another object, in saying these things. For since He was on the point of accusing them, that He might not seem in the sight of the foolish to set His heart on this authority of theirs, or for enmity to be doing these things, first He removed this thought, and having set himself clear from suspicion, then begins His accusation.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: And for what intent doth He convict them, and run out into a long discourse against them? To set the multitude on their guard, so that they might not fall into the same sins. For neither is dissuading like pointing out those that have offended; much as recommending what is right, is not like bringing forward those that have done well. For this cause also He is beforehand in saying, "Do not after their works." For, lest they should suppose, because of their listening to them, they ought also to imitate them, He uses this means of correction, and makes what seems to be their dignity a charge against them. For what can be more wretched than a teacher, when the preservation of his disciples is, not to give heed to his life? So that what seemeth to be their dignity is a most heavy charge against them, when they are shown to live such a life, as they that imitate are ruined.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: For this cause He also falls upon His accusations against them, but not for this only, but that He might show, that both their former unbelief wherewith they had not believed, and the crucifixion after this, which they dared to perpetrate, were not a charge against Him who was crucified and disbelieved, but against their perverseness.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But see whence He begins, and whence He aggravates His blame of them. "For they say," He saith, and do not." For every one is worthy of blame in transgressing the law, but especially he that bears the authority of teaching, for doubly and triply doth he deserve to be condemned. For one cause, because he transgresses; for another, that as he ought to amend others, and then halteth, he is worthy of a double punishment, because of his dignity; and in the third place, that he even corrupts the more, as committing such transgression in a teacher's place.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: The scribes and the Pharisees have sat upon the seat of Moses. All things therefore whatsoever they tell you to do, do. But do not do according to their works; for they say and do not do. They bind together heavy burdens and lay them upon men's shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them even with their finger.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Frequently indeed, but most of all in Matthew, it is observed that the disciples of Christ are better than the rest of the crowds. And you find indeed in the churches certain people who hear the divine teachings with love and who approach the word with more affection. Justly therefore are such men called disciples of Christ; but the many others who are not such are called his people.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And some things at times he speaks to his disciples alone and not also to the crowds, as those beatitudes written in the Gospel, concerning which Matthew indeed speaks thus: that seeing the crowds he went up into the mountain; and when he had sat down his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught them saying: blessed are the poor in spirit and the rest. But Luke says: lifting up his eyes upon his disciples he said: blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of heaven. But other things he announces to the crowds, as the parable of the sower declares.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And Matthew writes thus: but while he was speaking to the crowds, behold his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. To the crowds therefore he was speaking the things that are written before these; but when someone said to him: behold your mother and your brothers stand wishing to see you, answering the one who announced it to him he said: who is my mother, and my brothers? No longer stretching out his hand over the crowds, but over his disciples he said: behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever shall do the will of my Father who is in the heavens, he is to me both mother and brother.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And expounding the preceding parables Matthew writes: Jesus, having gone out of the house, was sitting beside the sea; and many crowds were gathered to him, so that going into a boat he sat, and all the people stood on the shore. And he spoke to them many things in parables, saying: behold, the sower went out to sow.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And lest you think that the narrative of the parable of the sower was so placed by chance, because Jesus was speaking it to the crowds, consider the exposition of Mark and Luke, who wrote similarly.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Mark indeed thus: he began again to teach beside the sea. And a great people was gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat and sat on the sea, and all the people was beside the sea on the land. And he taught them many things in parables, and said to them: the sower went out to sow. But Luke in this manner: when a great people was coming together and going out to him from the several cities, he spoke such a parable: the sower went out to sow his seed. But clearly knowing the difference between the people and the disciples, the evangelists after the parable added that now no longer to the crowds, but to the disciples he was expounding the cause on account of which he spoke to the crowds in parables.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Matthew indeed says thus: "the disciples coming said to him: why do you speak to them in parables?" But Luke thus: "his disciples asked him what this parable might be". But Mark: "and when they had come to be apart, the disciples asked him what this parable might be". And see whether you can from the Gospel of John hear and learn that those who only believe and do not desire to ascend in the word are the people of Christ, but those who are zealous for the better gifts and who, which is the first of all graces, study to receive "the word of wisdom" are his disciples.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But John says thus: that "Jesus said to those Jews who had believed: if you remain in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free". Therefore some things indeed he says to his disciples, some things to the crowds, but other things to the crowds together with the disciples, as also are these very present things concerning which we now speak.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Let us see therefore what he says "to the crowds and to the disciples": the scribes and the Pharisees have sat upon the seat of Moses. Which I judge to be of this sort: those who profess that they interpret the law of Moses and who glory in this, or those who profess to ascend above these things, these sit upon the seat of Moses. Those therefore who do not depart from the letter of the law are called scribes. But those who, professing something greater, separate themselves as if better from the many, according to this are called Pharisees, which is interpreted DIVIDED and SEGREGATED (for Phares is called DIVISION).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: It is therefore possible to see even now among the Jews scribes and Pharisees sitting upon the seat of Moses. I do not say this as though the scribes and Pharisees alone sat upon the seat of Moses, who said and did not do, and bound heavy burdens and unbearable ones upon the shoulders of men, but they themselves were unwilling to move them even with a finger. For I judge that those who understand and expound Moses according to the spiritual power sit indeed upon the seat of Moses, but are not scribes and Pharisees, but better than these. Such are the beloved disciples of Christ, who both interpret his word through the grace of God, and find those things which signify one thing from another.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore before the coming of Christ they indeed sat upon the seat of Moses well who interpreted the sayings of Moses well and according to reason. But after the coming of Christ they sit upon the seat of the Church, which is the seat of Christ and his throne.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But just as upon the seat of Moses the scribes and Pharisees sat badly, but those who rightly understood the law and handed it on sat well, so also upon the ecclesiastical seat there sit some who say what each one ought to do but do not themselves do it, and who, binding heavy burdens, lay them upon the shoulders of men, unwilling themselves to move them even with a finger, concerning whom the Savior said: "whoever shall loose one of these least commandments and shall teach men so, shall be called least in the kingdom of God". But others of those sitting do before they say, and speak wisely, moderating the differences of shoulders and laying burdens upon them sparingly. They themselves first move these burdens for the exhortation of the rest who hear, concerning whom the Lord says: "but he who shall do and teach so, he shall be called great in the kingdom of God".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The disciples of Christ are better than the common herd; and you may find in the Church such as with more ardent affection come to the word of God; these are Christ's disciples, the rest are only His people. And sometimes He speaks to His disciples alone, sometimes to the multitudes and His disciples together, as here.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: When the Lord had overthrown the Priests by His answer, and shown their condition to be irremediable, forasmuch as clergy, when they do wickedly, cannot be amended, but laymen who have gone wrong are easily set right, He turns His discourse to His Apostles and the people. For that is an unprofitable word which silences one, without conveying improvement to another.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: But further, if Christ reproves the scribes and Pharisees, sitting in the official chair of Moses, but not doing what they taught, what kind of (supposition).
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: Poemen also said, 'Teach your heart to follow what your tongue is saying to others.' He also said, 'Men try to appear excellent in preaching but they are less excellent in practising what they preach.'
paragraphs.author: Desert Fathers
paragraphs.work: The Desert Fathers, Sayings of the Early Christian Monks

paragraphs.text: (Chapter 23, Verses 1 and following.) Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: The scribes and Pharisees have seated themselves on the chair of Moses. Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do it, but do not do their works. For they speak, but do not practice. What is gentler, what is kinder than the Lord? He is tempted by the Pharisees, their plots are crushed, and according to the Psalmist: The arrows of little children have become their wounds (Psalms 63:8). And nevertheless, because of their priesthood and the dignity of their office, he urges the people to submit to them, considering not their works, but their teaching. But when He says, 'The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat,' He shows that the seat represents the teaching of the Law. Therefore, we must also understand the teaching in the passages that say, 'He did not sit on the throne of pestilence' (Psalms 1:1) and 'He overturned the seats of those selling doves' (Matthew 21:12; Mark 11:15).
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: The Scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat, as professing his Law, and boasting that they can interpret it. Those that do not depart from the letter of the Law are the Scribes; those who make high professions, and separate themselves from the vulgar as better than they, are called Pharisees, which signifies 'separate.' Those who understand and expound Moses according to his spiritual meaning, these sit indeed on Moses' seat, but are neither Scribes nor Pharisees, but better than either, Christ's beloved disciples. Since His coming these have sat upon the seat of the Church, which is the seat of Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But regard must be had to this, after what sort each man fills his seat; for not the seat makes the Priest, but the Priest the seat; the place does not consecrate the man, but the man the place. A wicked Priest derives guilt and not honour from his Priesthood.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (Chapter 23, Verses 1 and following.) Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: The scribes and Pharisees have seated themselves on the chair of Moses. Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do it, but do not do their works. For they speak, but do not practice. What is gentler, what is kinder than the Lord? He is tempted by the Pharisees, their plots are crushed, and according to the Psalmist: The arrows of little children have become their wounds (Psalms 63:8). And nevertheless, because of their priesthood and the dignity of their office, he urges the people to submit to them, considering not their works, but their teaching. But when He says, 'The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat,' He shows that the seat represents the teaching of the Law. Therefore, we must also understand the teaching in the passages that say, 'He did not sit on the throne of pestilence' (Psalms 1:1) and 'He overturned the seats of those selling doves' (Matthew 21:12; Mark 11:15).
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Hom. lxxii.) But that none should say, For this cause am I slack to practise, because my instructor is evil, He removes every such plea, saying, All therefore whatsoever they say unto you, that observe and do, for they speak not their own, but God's, which things He taught through Moses in the Law. And look with how great honour He speaks of Moses, showing again what harmony there is with the Old Testament.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Look with what He begins His reproof of them, For they say, and do not. Every one who transgresses the Law is deserving of blame, but especially he who has the post of instruction. And this for a threefold cause; first, because he is a transgressor; secondly, because when he ought to set others right, be himself halts; thirdly, because, being in the rank of a teacher, his influence is more corrupting.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Moreover, according to the simple sense of this saying where he says: do all things whatsoever they tell you to do, but do not do according to their works, we say that by these words he wishes to show that there are certain persons in the Church who, as far as speech is concerned, are indeed capable of teaching marvelous things and expound them according to reason, but are unwilling to act according to what they say: whose teaching indeed is to be heard, but whose manner of life is not to be imitated.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He therefore rebukes teachers of this kind, who not only do not do the things they teach, but also cruelly and without mercy, and not according to the estimation of the strength of each hearer, but greater than their power, impose burdens: for instance, those who forbid to marry and, away from what is expedient, compel people toward an immoderate purity, who also teach abstinence from foods and other things of this kind (to which faithful men ought not at all to be compelled), and who by the word of their exposition bind heavy burdens, contrary to the will of Christ who says: "my yoke is sweet and my burden is light", and lay them, as far as their word goes, upon the shoulders of men, bending them down and making them fall under the weight of grievous commandments — those who are not able to bear them up. And frequently one may see those who teach such things doing the contrary to their own words, and unwilling to move them even with a small strength of soul, which morally is called a finger.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For many, teaching chastity, have not kept chastity.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Exhorting others to abstain from foods, they themselves (whether for pretense or because they were overcome by their own concupiscences) have taken foods of this kind which they had renounced in words, teaching one thing in public and doing another secretly and covertly, doing all things for the sake of the persons of men and vain glories, as the following saying demonstrates, saying: they do all their works, that they may be seen by men. And for the most part all those are of this sort who love the first couches at banquets and greetings in the marketplace and to be called by men Rabbi, or something that is similar to this Rabbi: for instance, those who wish to be called bishops or presbyters or deacons, whereas each one of them, even if he were so called by someone, ought either to show his own conscience to God, that he does not wish to be named by this name of which he has neither the knowledge nor the practice.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if he does have it, nevertheless he ought not to wish to be called by that name which properly belongs to another. For the bishop, properly, is the Lord Jesus; and the presbyters are Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, as is manifest to those who consider the things written in Genesis concerning their seed, or the others who have been held worthy of this name, such as were the apostles of Christ; but the deacons are the seven archangels of God, to whose mysteries the seven deacons in the Acts have been ordained.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The Lord therefore cuts off concupiscences of this kind from our soul through these words which have been set down, and rather exhorts us to be zealous for humility, which is the first occasion of exaltation with God, just as, on the contrary, the occasion of humiliation with God is to love the first seats in the synagogues and the first couches at banquets and the first greetings in the marketplace and to be called Rabbi. And see that upon these things he adds and says: he who is greater among you, let him become a minister, and: he who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Thus from the phylacteries and fringes, made for the display of those who covet vain glories, and from their boastings for the sake of pomp, and from their garments and from their rings and their sandals, it is manifest who they are that love to be called Rabbi by men. If therefore (according to what we have said) the scribes and Pharisees sitting upon the seat of Moses are the teachers of the Jews, teaching the commandments of the law according to the letter, how does the Lord command us in the present words to do according to all things that they say, when all the apostles forbid the faithful to live according to the letter of the law, as the epistle of the apostles in the Acts testifies, which they sent to the Gentiles, that they should observe nothing from the law except what is sacrificed to idols and strangled, and fornication?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But those men teach the law according to the letter, not understanding the sense of the law spiritually, just as the apostle says of them: "but the end of the law is charity from a pure heart and faith unfeigned, from which certain men wandering away have turned aside to vain talk, wishing to be teachers of the law, understanding neither the things they speak, nor concerning what they affirm". For those who expound the law of Moses according to the letter, falling away from the love which is "from a pure heart and from faith unfeigned", in which the "spiritual law" is placed, are all vain-talkers.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For vain talk is circumcision, the unleavened bread, the passover, and the matter of clean and unclean things according to the letter of the law. These, therefore, who "have turned aside to vain talk and wish to be teachers of the law" and yet are not so according to the truth of the law, do indeed speak the commandments of the law, but do not understand the things they say, nor what the sayings of the law signify "concerning which they affirm".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore the Savior says of them: for they say and do not, for instance, they say concerning circumcision, concerning the passover, concerning the unleavened bread, concerning foods, concerning drinks, concerning festivals, concerning new moons, concerning sabbaths and the rest of the commandments of the law, but they do not do according to the will of the law. For they are not circumcised, as is the will of the law (whence the apostle says: "for we are the circumcision, we who serve God in the spirit and do not trust in the flesh"), nor do they sacrifice the passover (being ignorant that "our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed for us"), nor do they eat the unleavened bread according to the purpose of the law (which the apostle interprets, saying: "let us feast, not in the old leaven nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But neither do they celebrate the passover bodily, since the law commands that in Jerusalem, "the city which the Lord God has chosen", the lamb must be sacrificed, and that "three times in the year every male shall appear in the sight of the Lord God". But we who are disciples of Jesus, understanding those who sit upon the seat of Moses, the scribes and Pharisees, performing circumcisions and the other bodily commandments of the law, but set far off from the spiritual commandments of the law — whatsoever things they say to us out of the law, we, understanding the sense of the law, do and keep, by no means acting according to their works.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the things they speak, they seem indeed to say out of the law, yet they do not do as the law teaches.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For they neither receive charity in a pure heart, nor faith unfeigned, in which the sense of the law is placed, nor do they understand that there is a veil over the letter of the law, nor do they hear the prophet who understands this and at the same time asks: "unveil my eyes, and I will consider the marvelous things of your law". And thus they bind heavy burdens and (as Luke says) "unbearable ones", and lay them upon the shoulders of the disciples who listen to them. For the bodily commandments of the law according to the letter are heavy burdens and no light bindings, as Peter testifies in the Acts, saying: "why do you tempt God, and wish to impose a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But through the grace of God we believe that we are saved".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But its spiritual burden is light; therefore the Lord also says to those who were burdened and bound by the bodily commandments of the law: "come to me, you who labor and are heavy-laden, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and see, for my yoke is sweet and my burden is light". And the light burden is the Gospel, which is the spiritual law.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Moreover, the scribes and Pharisees sitting upon the seat of Moses do all their works, that they may be seen by men, receiving the visible circumcision and visibly removing the bodily leaven from their houses and in place of it likewise bringing in bodily unleavened bread, and seeking a Jerusalem visible to men and doing all things likewise to these. For they look upon "the things which are seen and are temporal", and they give alms that they may be glorified by men, and standing in the streets they pray, that they may be seen to be religious.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the true disciples of Christ, who look upon "the things which are not seen and are eternal", pray in their hidden storeroom and give alms in secret and fulfill the law in secret things, as Jews constituted in secret, according to what the apostle says: "for he is not a Jew who is so in the open, nor is that circumcision which is openly in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is so in secret, and circumcision is of the heart, which is in the spirit not the letter".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For in secret things and in invisible unleavened bread they feast "of sincerity and truth": they also eat the passover, Christ sacrificed for us, who said: "unless you eat my flesh, you have not eternal life in you". And by this, that they drink his blood, the true drink, they anoint the lintels of the houses of their soul, seeking not (as those men do) glory from men, but from God who sees the secret things.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if the Scribes and Pharisees who sit in Moses' seat are the teachers of the Jews, teaching the commandments of the Law according to the letter, how is this that the Lord bids us do after all things which they say; but the Apostles in the Acts forbid the believers to do according to the letter of the Law. (Acts 15:19.) These indeed taught after the letter, not understanding the Law spiritually.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Whatsoever they say to us out of the Law, with understanding of its sense, that we do and keep, not doing after their works, for they do not what the law enjoins, nor perceive the veil that is upon the letter of the Law. Or by all we are not to understand every thing in the Law, many things for example relating to the sacrifices, and the like, but such as concern our conduct. But why did He command this not of the Law of grace, but of the doctrine of Moses? Because truly it was not the time to publish the commandments of the New Law before the season of His passion.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: I think also that He had herein something further in view. He was about to bring many things against the Scribes and Pharisees in His discourse following, wherefore that vain men might not think that He coveted their place of authority, or spoke thus out of enmity to them, he first puts away from Himself this suspicion, and then begins to reprove them, that the people might not fall into their faults; and that, because they ought to hear them, they should not think that therefore they ought to imitate them in their works, He adds, But do ye not after their works. What can be more pitiable than such a teacher, whose life to imitate is ruin, to refuse to follow is salvation for his disciples?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But as gold is picked out of the dross, and the dross is left, so hearers may take doctrine and leave practice, for good doctrine oft comes from an evil man. But as Priests judge it better to teach the bad for the sake of the good, rather than to neglect the good for the sake of the bad; so also let those who are set under them pay respect to the bad Priests for the sake of the good, that the good may not be despised because of the bad; for it is better to give the bad what is not their due, rather than to defraud the good of what is justly theirs.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (Verse 4.) However, they bind heavy and burdensome loads and lay them on people's shoulders; but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger. This applies generally to all teachers who command heavy things but do not do smaller things. However, it should be noted that both the shoulders, the finger, the burdens, and the chains with which the burdens are bound should be understood spiritually.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But all these things, the shoulders, the finger, the burdens, and the bands with which they bind the burdens, have a spiritual meaning. Herein also the Lord speaks generally against all masters who enjoin high things, but do not even little things.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And together with these He mentions also another charge against them, that they are harsh to those accountable to them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: "For they bind heavy burdens, and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders, but they will not move them with their finger." He mentions here a twofold wickedness, their requiring great and extreme strictness of life, without any indulgence, from those over whom they rule, and their allowing to themselves great security; the opposite to which the truly good ruler ought to hold; in what concerns himself, to be an unpardoning and severe judge, but in the matters of those whom he rules, to be gentle and ready to make allowances; the contrary to which was the conduct of these men.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: For such are all they who practise self restraint in mere words, unpardoning and grievous to bear as having no experience of the difficulty in actions. And this itself too is no small fault, and in no ordinary way increases the former charge.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But do thou mark, I pray thee, how He aggravates this accusation also. For He did not say, "they cannot," but, "they will not." And He did not say, "to bear," but, "to move with a finger," that is, not even to come near them, nor to touch them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: And to the Scribes and Pharisees of whom He is now speaking, heavy burdens not to be borne are the commandments of the Law; as St. Peter speaks in the Acts, Why seek ye to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? (Acts 15:10.) For commending the burdens of the Law by fabulous proofs, they bound as it were the shoulders of the heart of their hearers with bands, that thus tied as though with proof of reason to them, they might not fling them off; but themselves did not in the least measure fulfil them, that is, not only did not wholly, but did not so much as attempt to.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Such also are they who lay a heavy burden upon those who come to penitence, so that while men would avoid present punishment, they overlook that which is to come. For if you lay upon a boy's shoulders a burden more than he can bear, he must needs cither cast it off, or be broken down by it; so the man on whom you lay too grievous a burden of penance must either wholly refuse it, or if he submit himself to it will find himself unable to bear it, and so be offended, and sin worse. Also, if we should be wrong in imposing too light a penance, is it not better to have to answer for mercy than for severity? Where the master of the household is liberal, the steward should not be oppressive.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: If God be kind, should His Priest be harsh? Do you seek thereby the character of sanctity? Be strict in ordering your own life, in that of others lenient; let men hear of you as enjoining little, and performing much. The Priest who gives licence to himself, and exacts the utmost from others, is like a corrupt tax-gatherer in the state, who to ease himself taxes others heavily.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Three brothers once came to a hermit in Scetis. One of them said to him, 'Abba, I have memorized the Old and New Testaments.' But the hermit answered, 'And you have filled the air with words.' The second said to him, 'I have written out the Old and New Testaments with my own hand.' But the hermit said, 'And you have filled the window-ledge with manuscripts.' The third said, 'The grass is growing up my chimney.' But the hermit answered, 'And you have driven away hospitality.'
paragraphs.author: Desert Fathers
paragraphs.work: The Desert Fathers, Sayings of the Early Christian Monks

paragraphs.text: (Verse 6.) For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplaces, and to be called Rabbi by men. Woe to us, miserable ones, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have been passed on. When the Lord gave the commandments of the Law through Moses, He added at the end: Bind them upon your hand, and they shall be before your eyes (Deut. VI, 8). And the meaning is: Let my precepts be in your hand, so that they may be fulfilled in action: let them be before your eyes, so that day and night you may meditate on them. The Pharisees, by misinterpreting this, wrote the Ten Commandments of Moses on scrolls, folding them up and binding them on their foreheads, making them like a crown on their heads so that they would always be before their eyes. This is still done today by the Indians, Persians, and Babylonians, and those who do this are considered religious among the people.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Moses also commanded (Num. XV) that the Israelite people should make blue tassels on the corners of their garments, to distinguish them as the chosen people, just as circumcision is a sign for the Jewish people's bodies, so their clothing should have some distinction. Superstitious teachers, seeking popular applause, and pursuing gains from women, made large phylacteries and bound the sharpest thorns in them so that, as they walked or sat, they would be punctured and, as it were, be drawn by this admonition to the duties of the Lord and to the ministries of his service.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Therefore, because the Lord had said that they do all their works to be seen by men, which he had accused in general, he now divides them into parts. Those little tablets of the Decalogue were called phylacteries, which whoever had them would have as a safeguard and a reminder of themselves: the Pharisees not understanding that these things should be carried in the heart, not on the body; otherwise, even cabinets and chests have books, but do not have knowledge of God. This is done among us by superstitious women, in little Gospels, and in the wood of the cross, and in similar things (which indeed they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge).
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Romans 10) Even today, they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (Below, in the same place). Such was the fringe, small and short, from the Law and the precepts, which was touched by the woman who was flowing with blood, in the cloak of the Lord (Luke 8, above).
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But she was not moved by the superstitious thorns of the Pharisees; rather, she was healed by touching it. And when they excessively enlarge their phylacteries and make large fringes, seeking glory from men, they are accused in the rest, why they seek the first places at dinners, and the first seats in synagogues; and in public they cut throats and glory; and they are called Rabbi by men, which is said in Latin language, teacher....
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Verse 5.) All their works they do to be seen by others. Therefore, whoever does anything to be seen by others, is a scribe and a Pharisee.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: For the Lord, when He had given the commandments of the Law through Moses, added at the end, And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be ever before thine eyes; (Deut. 6:8.) the meaning of which is, Let my precepts be in thine hand so as to be fulfilled in thy works; let them be before thine eyes so as that thou shalt meditate upon them day and night.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: This the Pharisees misinterpreting, wrote on parchments the Decalogue of Moses, that is, the Ten Commandments, and folding them up, tied them on their forehead, so making them a crown for their head, that they should be always before their eyes. Moses had in another place given command that they should make fringes of blue in the borders of their garments, to distinguish the people of Israel (Numb. 15:39.); that as in their bodies circumcision, so in their garments the fringe, might discriminate the Jewish nation.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But these superstitious teachers, catching at popular favour, and making gain of silly women, made broad hems, and fastened them with sharp pins, that as they walked or sat they might be pricked, and by such monitors be recalled to the duties of God's ministry. This embroidery then of the Decalogue they called phylacteries, that is, conservatories, because those who wore them, wore them for their own protection and security. So little did the Pharisees understand that they were to be worn on the heart and not on the body; for in equal degree may cases and chests be said to have books, which assuredly have not the knowledge of God.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But wherein are they earnest, and vigorous? In the things forbidden. For, "all their works they do," He saith, "to be seen of men." These things He saith, accusing them in respect of vainglory, which kind of thing was their ruin. For the things before were signs of harshness and remissness, but these of the mad desire of glory.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: This drew them off from God, this caused them to strive before other spectators, and ruined them. For whatever kind of spectators any one may have, since it hath become his study to please these, such also are the contests he exhibits And he that wrestles among the noble, such also are the conflicts he takes in hand, but he among the cold and supine, himself also becomes more remiss. For instance, hath any one a beholder that delights in ridicule? he himself too becomes a mover of ridicule, that he may delight the spectator: hath another one who is earnest minded, and practises self-government? he endeavors himself to be such as he is, since such is the disposition of him who praises him.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But see again that here too the charge is with aggravation. For neither is it that they do some things in this way, some in another way, but all things absolutely this way.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: Then, having blamed them for vainglory, He shows that it is not even about great and necessary things they are vainglorious (for neither had they these, but were destitute of good works), but for things without warmth or worth, and such as were certain proofs of their baseness, the phylacteries, the borders; of their garments. "For they make broad their phylacteries," He saith, "and enlarge the borders of their garments."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: And what are these phylacteries, and these borders? Since they were continually forgetting God's benefits, He commanded His marvellous works to be inscribed on little tablets, and that these should be suspended from their hands (wherefore also He said, "They shall be immoveable in thine eyes"), which they called phylacteries; as many of our women now wear Gospels hung from their necks. And in order that by another thing again they may be reminded, like as many often do, binding round their finger with a piece of linen or a thread, as being likely to forget, this God enjoined them as children to do, "to sew a ribbon of blue on their garments, upon the fringe that hung round their feet, that they might look at it, and remember the commandments;" and they were called "borders."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: In these things then they were diligent, making wide the strips of the tablets, and enlarging the borders of their garments; which was a sign of the most extreme vanity. For wherefore art thou vainglorious, and dost make these wide? what, is this thy good work? what cloth it profit thee at all, if thou gain not the good results from them. For God seeks not the enlarging of these and making them wide, but our remembering His benefits. But if for almsgiving and prayer, although they be attended with labor, and be good deeds on our parts, we must not seek vainglory, how dost thou, O Jew, pride thyself in these things, which most of all convict thy remissness.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: And their works likewise they do to be seen of men, using outward circumcision, taking away actual leaven out of their houses, and doing such like things. But Christ's disciples fulfil the Law in things secret, being Jews inwardly, as the Apostle speaks. (Rom. 2:29.)
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: After this let us see what it means when he says: they make broad their phylacteries and enlarge the fringes of their garments. It must be understood in these matters that it is written in the law concerning the divine words, saying: "bind them upon your hand, and they shall be moving before your eyes". Those, therefore, who do all things in order to be seen by men, the scribes and Pharisees, writing certain sayings of the law on two cut pieces of parchment, bind them, and one indeed they carry on their houses, as it were placing upon their heads as a crown that which is written according to the forehead. But the other upon the arm of their hand; and they call them "phylacteries". Similarly, finding something also about the fringe in Deuteronomy, they suppose that they keep the law by making some fringe on some part of the garments which they wear.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore, reproving these things too in the scribes and Pharisees, in their bodily and visible observances, the Lord says: they do all things in order to be seen by men. For they make broad their phylacteries and enlarge the fringes of their garments. But the disciples of Jesus do all their works in order to be seen by God alone; for they bind the law of God upon their hand, spiritually upon their good work, and by meditation on the divine teachings, ever moving them, they make the divine precepts moving before the eyes of their souls, and the fringe full of the virtue of Jesus — in this, that they imitate the Master.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Every substance breeds in itself that which destroys it, as wood the worm, and garments the moth; so the Devil strives to corrupt the ministry of the Priests, who are ordained for the edification of holiness, endeavouring that this good, while it is done to be seen of men, should be turned into evil. Take away this fault from the clergy, and you will have no further labour in their reform, for of this it comes that a clergyman who has sinned can hardly perform penance.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Also the Lord here points out the cause why they could not believe in Christ, because nearly all they did was in order to be seen of men; for he whose desire is for earthly glory from men, cannot believe on Christ who preaches things heavenly. I have read one who interprets this place thus. In Moses' seat, that is, in the rank and degree instituted by Moses, the Scribes and Pharisees are seated unworthily, forasmuch as they preached to others the Law which foretold Christ's coming, but themselves did not receive Him when come. For this cause He exhorts the people to hear the Law which they preached, that is, to believe in Christ who was preached by the Law, but not to follow the Scribes and Pharisees in their disbelief of Him. And He shows the reason why they preached the coming of Christ out of the Law, yet did not believe on Him; namely, because they did not preach that Christ should come through any desire of His coming, but that they might be seen by men to be doctors of the Law.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: But after their example do many invent Hebrew names of Angels, and write them, and bind them on themselves, and they seem dreadful to such as are without understanding. Others again wear round their neck a portion of the Gospel written out. But is not the Gospel read every day in the Church, and heard by all? Those therefore who receive no profit from the Gospel sounded in their ears, how shall the having them hung about their neck save them? Further, wherein is the virtue of the Gospel? in the shape of its letters, or in the understanding its meaning?
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: If in the characters, you do well to hang them round your neck; if in their meaning, they are of more profit when laid up in the heart, than hung round the neck. But others explain this place thus, That they made broad their teachings concerning special observances, as phylacteries, or preservatives of salvation, preaching them continually to the people. And the broad fringes of their garments they explain of the same undue stress upon such commandments.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (Verse 6.) For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplaces, and to be called Rabbi by men. Woe to us, miserable ones, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have been passed on. When the Lord gave the commandments of the Law through Moses, He added at the end: Bind them upon your hand, and they shall be before your eyes (Deut. VI, 8). This is still done today by the Indians, Persians, and Babylonians, and those who do this are considered religious among the people.

paragraphs.text: (Romans 10) Even today, they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (Below, in the same place). Such was the fringe, small and short, from the Law and the precepts, which was touched by the woman who was flowing with blood, in the cloak of the Lord (Luke 8, above). But she was not moved by the superstitious thorns of the Pharisees; rather, she was healed by touching it. And when they excessively enlarge their phylacteries and make large fringes, seeking glory from men, they are accused in the rest, why they seek the first places at dinners, and the first seats in synagogues; and in public they cut throats and glory; and they are called Rabbi by men, which is said in Latin language, teacher. Denique sequitur:
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Seeing they thus make broad their phylacteries, and make them broad fringes, desiring to have glory of men, they are convicted also in other things; For they love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But they not in these only, but in other little things, suffered from this disease.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: For, "they love," He saith, "the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi." For these things, although one may think them small, yet are they a cause of great evils. These things have overthrown both cities and churches.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: And it comes upon me now even to weep, when I hear of the first seats, and the greetings, and consider how many ills were hence engendered to the churches of God, which it is not necessary to publish to you now; nay rather as many as are aged men do not even need to learn these things from us.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But mark thou, I pray thee, how vainglory prevailed; when they were commanded not to be vainglorious, even in the synagogues, where they had entered to discipline others.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: For to have this feeling at feasts, to howsoever great a degree, doth not seem to be so dreadful a thing; although even there the teachers ought to be held in reverence, and not in the church only, but everywhere. And like as a man, wherever he may appear, is manifestly distinguished from the brutes; so also ought the teacher, both speaking and holding his peace, and dining, and doing whatever it may be, to be distinguished as well by his gait, as by his look, and by his garb, and by all things generally. But they were on every account objects of ridicule, and in every respect disgraced themselves, making it their study to follow what they ought to flee. For they love them, it is said; but if the loving them be a matter of blame, what a thing must the doing them be; and to hunt and strive after them, how great an evil.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But what should be said of those who love the first couches at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues and the first greetings in the marketplace and to be called Rabbi by men? Clearly offenses of this kind were found, and are found, not only among the scribes and Pharisees of that time alone, but even in the Church of Christ there are found not only banquets, and those who, undertaking the tables of those who provide them, but also those who love the first seats at them and do many things — first, indeed, that they may become deacons (not such as Scripture describes, but such as are "those who devour the houses of widows, praying at length for a pretext," and who for this reason "shall receive the greater judgment").
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And those who wish to become deacons of this sort consequently strive to seize beforehand the visible first seats of those who are called presbyters.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Some, however, not content even with these, contrive very many things, so that they may be called bishops by men (which is Rabbi), when they ought to understand that a bishop must become "beyond reproach" and the rest of the things that follow, so that even if he is not said to be a bishop by men, he may nevertheless be one before God. For he who has in himself the things which Paul enumerates concerning a bishop, even if he is not a bishop before men, is a bishop before God — even if he has not come to that rank through the ordination of men. For in this way a man is a physician who has learned the medical discipline and is able to heal as a physician: even if the sick do not entrust their bodies to him, he is a physician.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But also a man is a pilot who has learned the pilot's art and is able to use it as is fitting: even if no one has entrusted to him the helm of a ship, he is nevertheless a pilot.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But you will find lovers of new glory who are zealous for glory from men and do not desire it from God; and, as it were, some men are brought before them as before judges and governors; and, if it must be said, through this very thing they make Christ's lightest burden an intolerable burden. But the disciple of Christ bears with it and still intercedes and does all things that he may be seen by God, despising human glory.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He, seeing the suppers of the Gospel parables and the heavenly churches and assemblies and fairs of the firstborn, in which was (according to the Song of Songs) the bride, loves indeed at the spiritual suppers the first couches, that he may eat the better portions of the spiritual foods and the first-fruits of the spiritual banquet, and not the leftovers of the rest. He loves also, with the apostles sitting "upon twelve thrones", the first seats, hastening to render himself worthy by good deeds of seats of this kind; and so too the greetings which take place in the fairs, which we explained above.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the just man loves to be called Rabbi neither by men nor by any other, certain that there is one master of all. And all who are under him are, one toward another, brothers. But also he who by a heavenly birth has been born not only "of water" but also "of the Spirit", and has received "the spirit of adoption", so that it may be said of him that he was born not "of flesh" "nor of the will of man but of God", still being the son of none of those who are reckoned on earth and below, does not call anyone father on earth, as one who through every deed accomplished according to God says "our Father, who art in heaven". And if anyone ministers the divine words, he by no means offers himself to be called master, as one knowing that Christ is in him when he has made good progress, whom it behooves to be called master by all who have been benefited, but he professes himself a minister according to the commandment of Christ, who says: he who is greater among you, let him be the minister of all. Since Christ himself also, though he was truly master, professed himself to be a minister, saying: "but I am in the midst of you, not as one who reclines at table, but as one who ministers."
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But well, after all the things by which he forbade the desires of vainglory, did he add, saying: he who exalts himself shall be humbled. Would that all indeed heard this, but most of all deacons and presbyters and bishops — most of all those who suppose that these things are not written for them: he who exalts himself shall be humbled. For which reason, as though not knowing that other saying either, he who humbles himself shall be exalted, they do not hear him who said: "learn of me, for I am gentle and humble of heart".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But they are puffed up, and through their inflation they fall "into the judgment of the devil", and they do not seek through humility to ascend from the judgment of inflation, when they ought to remember the word of wisdom which says: "the greater you are, the more humble yourself, and before God you will find grace". And this the Lord first fulfilled; for as much as he had been great, so much did he humble himself. For "though" he "was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of man; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself even unto death, and death of the cross. For which reason God also exalted him above all, and gave him a name which is above every name" and the rest.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For He rebukes not those who recline in the highest place, but those who love such places, blaming the will not the deed. For to no purpose does he humble himself in place who exalts himself in heart. For some vain men hearing that it was a commendable thing to seat himself in the lowest place, chooses so to do; and thus not only does not put away the vanity of his heart, but adds this additional vain ostentation of his humility, as one who would be thought righteous and humble. For many proud men take the lowest place in their bodies, but in haughtiness of heart think themselves to be seated among the highest; and there are many humble men who, placed among the highest, are inwardly in their own esteem among the lowest.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: It should be noted, that He does not forbid those to whom this belongs by right of rank to be saluted in the forum, or to sit or recline in the highest room; but those who unduly desire these things, whether they obtain them or not, these He enjoins the believers to shun as wicked.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: They love the first salutations, first, that is, not in time only, before others; but in tone, that we should say with a loud voice, Hail, Rabbi; and in body that we should bow low our head; and in place, that the salutation should be in public.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: That is, they wish to be called, not to be such; they desire the name, and neglect the duties.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: And herein they are not without fault, that the same men should be concerned in the litigations of the forum, who in the synagogue in Moses' seat, seek to be called Rabbi by men.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: (Verse 8 onwards) But you must not be called Rabbi; for One is your Teacher, and you are all brothers. And do not call anyone on earth your father; for One is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor are you to be called teachers; for One is your Teacher, the Christ. But the greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted. Neither be called masters; for One is your Master, that is, Christ. And do not call anyone on earth your father; for One is your Father, He who is in heaven.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Father, because from Him all things are. Teacher, because through Him all things: or because through the dispensation of His flesh, we all are reconciled to God. It is asked why the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, declared himself to be against this precept (2 Corinthians 5; Colossians 1); or how, in the common language, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, they call each other Fathers? This is resolved as follows: It is one thing to be a father or a teacher by nature, another thing by indulgence.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: If we call someone our father, we show honor to their age, not that they are the author of our life. Likewise, a teacher is called such from the fellowship of a true teacher. And to avoid endless repetition, just as one God and one Son do not prejudice others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so one father and one teacher do not prejudice others from being called fathers and teachers in an abusive manner.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (cont. Helvid. 15.) All men may be called brethren in affection, which is of two kinds, general and particular. Particular, by which all Christians are brethren; general, by which all men being born of one Father are bound together by like tie of kindred.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: The other things then He carried no further than to accuse them, as being small and trifling, and as though His disciples needed not at all to be corrected about these matters; but what was a cause of all the evils, even ambition, and the violent seizing of the teacher's chair, this He brings forward, and corrects with diligence, touching this vehemently and earnestly charging them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: For what saith He? "But be not ye called Rabbi." Then follows the cause also; "For one is your master, and all ye are brethren;" and one hath nothing more than another, in respect of his knowing nothing from himself. Wherefore Paul also saith, "For who is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers?" He said not masters.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: And in the Church of Christ are found some who take to themselves the uppermost places, that is, become deacons; next they aspire to the chief seats of those that are called presbyters; and some intrigue to be styled among men Bishop, that is, to be called Rabbi. But Christ's disciple loves the uppermost place indeed, but at the spiritual banquet, where he may feed on the choicer morsels of spiritual food, for, with the Apostles who sit upon twelve thrones, he loves the chief seats, and hastes by his good works to render himself worthy of such seats; and he also loves salutations made in the heavenly market-place, that is, in the heavenly congregations of the primitive. But the righteous man would be called Rabbi, neither by man, nor by any other, because there is One Master of all men.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Be not ye called Rabbi, that ye take not to yourselves what belongs to God. And call not others Rabbi, that ye pay not to men a divine honour. For One is the Master of all, who instructs all men by nature. For if man were taught by man, all men would learn that have teachers; but seeing it is not man that teaches, but God, many are taught, but few learn. Man cannot by teaching impart an understanding to man, but that understanding which is given by God man calls forth
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: So, too, righteousness-for the God of righteousness and of creation is the same-was first in a rudimentary state, having a natural fear of God: from that stage it advanced, through the Law and the Prophets, to infancy; from that stage it passed, through the Gospel, to the fervour of youth: now, through the Paraclete, it is settling into maturity. He will be, after Christ, the only one to be called and revered as Master; for He speaks not from Himself, but what is commanded by Christ.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: Therefore a wife, when her husband is dead, will not marry; for if she marry, she will of course be marrying (his) brother: for "all we are brethren." Again, the woman, if intending to marry, has to marry "in the Lord; " that is, not to an heathen, but to a brother, inasmuch as even the ancient law forbids marriage with members of another tribe.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: And that the disciples may ever remember that they are the children of one parent, and that by their new birth they have passed the limits of their earthly origin.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 8 onwards) But you must not be called Rabbi; for One is your Teacher, and you are all brothers. And do not call anyone on earth your father; for One is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor are you to be called teachers; for One is your Teacher, the Christ. But the greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted. Neither be called masters; for One is your Master, that is, Christ. And do not call anyone on earth your father; for One is your Father, He who is in heaven.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Father, because from Him all things are. Teacher, because through Him all things: or because through the dispensation of His flesh, we all are reconciled to God. It is asked why the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, declared himself to be against this precept (2 Corinthians 5; Colossians 1); or how, in the common language, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, they call each other Fathers? This is resolved as follows: It is one thing to be a father or a teacher by nature, another thing by indulgence.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: If we call someone our father, we show honor to their age, not that they are the author of our life. Likewise, a teacher is called such from the fellowship of a true teacher. And to avoid endless repetition, just as one God and one Son do not prejudice others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so one father and one teacher do not prejudice others from being called fathers and teachers in an abusive manner.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: It is a difficulty that the Apostle against this command calls himself the teacher of the Gentiles; and that in monasteries in their common conversation, they call one another, Father. It is to be cleared thus. It is one thing to be father or master by nature, another by sufferance. Thus when we call any man our father, we do it to show respect to his age, not as regarding him as the author of our being. We also call men 'Master,' from resemblance to a real master; and, not to use tedious repetition, as the One God and One Son, who are by nature, do not preclude us from calling others gods and sons by adoption, so the One Father and One Master, do not preclude us from speaking of other fathers and masters by an abuse of the terms.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Not that when Christ is here said to be our Master, the Father is excluded, as neither when God is said to be our Father, is Christ excluded, Who is the Father of men.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Seest thou not those who adopt to themselves sons here, how they commit not the act to slaves, but are themselves present at the judgment-seat? Even so neither hath God committed His gift to angels, but Himself is present, commanding and saying, "Call no man Father on earth;" not that thou shouldest dishonor them that gave thee birth, but that thou shouldest prefer to all those Him that made thee, and enrolled thee amongst His own children. For He that hath given the greater, that is, hath set Himself before thee, much more will He not think scorn to distribute unto thee of His body.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 50

paragraphs.text: And again, "Call not, father," not that they should not call, but they may know whom they ought to call Father, in the highest sense. For like as the master is not a master principally; so neither is the father. For He is cause of all, both of the masters, and of the fathers.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But who calls no man father upon earth? He who in every action done as before God, says, Our Father, which art in Heaven.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And call no man your Father upon earth; because in this world though man begets man, yet there is one Father who created all men. For we have not beginning of life from our parents, but we have our life transmitted through them.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Why not? He had found the son whom he had lost; he had felt him to be all the dearer of whom he had made a gain. Who is that father to be understood by us to be? God, surely: no one is so truly a Father; no one so rich in paternal love.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: However, our Lord very frequently proclaimed God as a Father to us; nay, even gave a precept "that we call no one on earth father, but the Father whom we have in the heavens: and so, in thus praying, we are likewise obeying the precept.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: To Abraham, in fine, they appeal; prohibited though they are to acknowledge any other father than God. Grant, now, that Abraham is our father; grant, too, that Paul is.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: And again He adds, "Neither be ye called guides, for one is your guide, even Christ;" and He said not, I. For like as above He said, "What think ye of Christ?" and He said not, "of me," so here too.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: But I should be glad to ask here, what they would say, who are repeatedly applying the term one, one, to the Father alone, to the rejection of the Only-begotten. Is the Father guide? All would declare it, and none would gainsay it. And yet "one," He saith, "is your guide, even Christ." For like as Christ, being called the one guide, casts not out the Father from being guide; even so the Father, being called Master, doth not cast out the Son from being Master. For the expression, one, one, is spoken in contra-distinction to men, and the rest of the creation.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: Since those who have arrived teaching new beliefs for the most part do so from conceit and arrogance, I will say something concerning the value of the teaching. The Lord cuts short this opinion and way as leading to destruction. He says, "You love glory and the places of first importance." Meanwhile he desires the servant's role and cultivates humility.
paragraphs.author: Cyril of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Having warned them therefore against this grievous pest, and amended them, He instructs also how they may escape it; by humility. Wherefore He adds also, "He that is greatest among you shall be your servant. For whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased, and whosoever shall abase himself shall be exalted."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: For nothing is equal to the practice of modesty, wherefore He is continually reminding them of this virtue, both when He brought the children into the midst, and now. And, when on the mount, beginning the beatitudes, He began from hence. And in this place, He plucks it up by the roots hereby, saying, "He that abaseth himself shall be exalted."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: Seest thou how He draws off the hearer right over to the contrary thing. For not only doth He forbid him to set his heart upon the first place, but requires him to follow after the last. For so shalt thou obtain thy desire, He saith. Wherefore he that pursues his desire for the first, must follow after the last place. "For he that abaseth himself shall be exalted."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

paragraphs.text: Or otherwise; And if one minister the divine word, knowing that it is Christ that makes it to be fruitful, such a one professes himself a minister and not a master; whence it follows, He that is greatest among you, let him be your servant. As Christ Himself, who was in truth our Master, professed Himself a minister, saying, I am in the midst of you as one that ministers. (Luke 22:27.) And well does He conclude this prohibition of all vain-glory with the words, And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: A hermit said, 'He who is praised and honoured above what he deserves suffers grievous loss. He who receives no honour at all among men, shall be glorified hereafter.'
paragraphs.author: Desert Fathers
paragraphs.work: The Desert Fathers, Sayings of the Early Christian Monks

paragraphs.text: Which means that every one who thinks highly of his own deserts, shall be humbled before God; and every one who humbles himself concerning his good deeds, shall be exalted with God.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: "Woe" is a voice of sorrowing. For this reason he says that they close the kingdom of heaven, because they hide in the law the consolation of his truth. They lost sight of the advent expected by the prophets. Through deceptive teachings, they do not allow others to go to heaven either. They do not adorn the way of eternity.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Ver. 13, 14.) But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows' houses and for a pretense you make long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater condemnation. The scribes and Pharisees have knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, and they know that Christ is the Son of God; they are not ignorant that He was born of a Virgin. But while they seek to prey on the subject people, they themselves do not enter the kingdom of heaven, nor do they allow those who could enter to do so. This is what the Prophet Hosea accuses: The priests have hidden the way, they have murdered Shechem (Hosea 6:9). And again: The priests have not said, 'Where is the Lord?' (Hosea 4). Indeed, every teacher who scandalizes his disciples with evil deeds shuts the kingdom of heaven before them.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "Woe unto you, for ye shut up the kingdom against men; for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in." But if to profit no one be a charge against a man, even to hurt and hinder, what plea hath that? But what means, "them that are entering in?" Them that are fit for it. For when they were to lay injunctions on others, they used to make the burdens intolerable, but when they themselves were to do any of the things required, on the contrary, so far from doing anything, they went much beyond this in wickedness, they even used to corrupt others. These are they that are called pests, who make their employment the ruin of others, standing right contrary to teachers. For if it be the part of a teacher to save that which is perishing, to destroy that which is on the point of being saved is that of a destroyer.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: Christ is truly the Son of that God Who gave the Law; after the example of the blessings pronounced in the Law, did Himself pronounce the blessings of them that are saved; and also after the cursings of the Law, He now sets forth a woe against sinners; Woe unto you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites. They who allow that it is compatible with goodness to utter these denunciations against sinners, should understand that the purpose of God is the same in the cursings of the Law. Both the cursing there and the woe here fall upon the sinner not from Him who denounces, but from themselves who commit the sins which are denounced, and worthily bring upon themselves the inflictions of God's discipline, appointed for the turning of men to good. So a father rebuking a son utters words of cursing, but does not desire that he should become deserving of those curses, but rather that he should turn himself from them. He adds the cause of this woe, Ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men; for ye neither go in yourselves, nor suffer them that are entering to go in. These two commandments are by nature inseparable; because not to suffer others to enter in, is of itself enough to keep the hinderer out.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
