paragraphs.text: The Pharisees and the Scribes then would neither enter in, nor hear Him who said, By me if any man enter in he shall be saved; (John 10:9.) nor would they suffer those to enter in, who were able to have believed through the things which had been spoken before by the Law and the Prophets concerning Christ, but shut up the door with every kind of device to deter men from entering. Also they detracted from His teaching, denied all prophecy concerning Him, and blasphemed every miracle as deceitful, or wrought by the Devil.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: All who in their evil conversation set an example of sinning to the people, and who commit injustice, offending the weak, seem to shut up the kingdom of heaven before men. And this sin is found among the people, and chiefly among the doctors, when they teach men what the Gospel righteousness requires of them, but do not what they teach.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But those who both teach and live well open to men the kingdom of heaven, and both enter in themselves, and invite others to enter in. Many also will not suffer those who are willing to enter into the kingdom of heaven, when they without reason excommunicate out of jealousy others who are better than themselves; thus they refuse them entrance, but these of sober spirit, overcoming by their patience this tyranny, although forbidden, yet enter in and inherit the kingdom.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Also they who with much rashness have set themselves to the profession of teaching before they have learned, and following Jewish fables, detract from those who search out the higher things of Scripture; these do, as far as in them lies, shut out men from the kingdom of heaven.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before men; for you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Those who dare to call God not good on account of the curses which God set down against sinners in his law — let them hear how, as truly the Son of that God who gave the law, in likeness indeed of the blessings which are set down in the law, he too pronounces the beatitudes of those who are saved, but in likeness of the curses set down in the law he sets woe against sinners, saying: woe to you and to you. And let those who bring a charge against the God of the law, hearing these things, not understanding that those things too were spoken by a kindly God, say what we ought to understand concerning Jesus when he says: woe to you, scribes and Pharisees. Those who confess that it belongs to goodness to pronounce such things against sinners — let them understand that the purpose of God is the same in bringing forth the curses of the law within the law. But whether it be that curse or this pronounced woe — it befalls each sinner not from the pronouncement of the one pronouncing, but from the sins of the sinner himself, who offers himself worthy for the reception either of those curses or of these woes, which God pronounced for the sake of discipline against those men, that he might turn them to the good. For a father too, rebuking his son, frequently brings forth for his amendment certain words which seem to be curses, and yet he does not wish him to become worthy of those curses, but rather desires to turn him away from them.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: We have said these things in order to show that the Gospels are in agreement with the law. So too now, when he says woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you shut the kingdom of heaven, he terrified the scribes and Pharisees, that they might not mock the kingdom of heaven before men. But the scribes and Pharisees shutting the kingdom of heaven offend in two ways at once: in one indeed that they themselves do not enter into the kingdom of heaven, and secondly that those entering they do not allow to enter. These two sins are by nature inseparable from one another. For whoever sins in one of these cannot abstain from the other.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Likewise, conversely, whoever abstains from the one, it is impossible that he should not also abstain from the other; for instance, no one is found who, himself entering into the kingdom of heaven, does not permit others to enter, since for him who forbids others to enter into the kingdom this very thing — that he does not permit others to enter — suffices for his own expulsion, so that he does not enter into the kingdom of heaven; for whoever "shall scandalize one of the little ones" of the Church, forbidding anyone to enter into the kingdom of heaven, will suffer what is written in the Gospel, woe. Likewise, conversely, whoever is able to make someone enter into the kingdom of heaven — if indeed it is within his power both to permit and to forbid — much more will he himself enter into the kingdom of heaven.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Since the Lord frequently says woe to the scribes and Pharisees, we will set out the cause of each woe in its proper place.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But now let us set out the cause of this present woe. The cause, then, of the present woe is that they were shutting up the kingdom of heaven before men; and in shutting it before others, they themselves did not enter, precisely because they forbade to enter those who would surely have entered, if they had not been shut out by these men. And first, indeed, the present passage is to be expounded simply, as of the scribes and Pharisees who are found among the Jews. For these men, not content that they themselves did not believe the Lord, went still further and disparaged his teaching and overthrew every prophecy written concerning him and blasphemed his every work as false and feigned by the devil, saying, "this man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul", and showed themselves murderous toward those who had believed in Christ, and in every way forbade anyone to come to Christianity, through which one enters into the kingdom of heaven.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: They were shutting up that which had been openly announced and preached in the sight of all and proclaimed aloud among all men. And in shutting up the kingdom of heaven they themselves did not enter (for neither did they wish to hear him who said: "if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved, and shall go in and go out and find pasture"); and those entering (that is, those who could believe on account of the faith which "from the law and the prophets" had earlier been declared concerning Christ) they did not permit to enter. Utterly breaking up the very beginning of their assent, and with all terror and savage boldness, as far as lay in them, they themselves, by shutting the door, forbade all who wished to enter through the door.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: To this simple exposition we will join also this, concerning those who sin among us. For all who by an evil manner of life urge on an example of sinning among the people, and who do injury to those who are still little ones in Christ and imperfect, disheartening and scandalizing them, seem to shut the kingdom of heaven before men, and neither do they themselves enter nor do they permit others to enter.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And this sin is found indeed even among the common people, but most of all among the teachers, who indeed teach men according to the justice of the Gospel, but do not do what they teach, because they are evil shepherds and therefore do not spare the sheep nor care for their salvation, but always look to the gains coming to them from men in return for the fact that they seem to feed the people when they do not feed them, and are caught in filthy gains and in the lusts of empty glory.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For these are the wages of the hirelings, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men and do not enter into it, nor do they wish to understand what is said: "strive to enter through the narrow door". And since above all contests this is the contest, that one should be doing violence and seizing the heavenly kingdom, to such teachers, then, these words are fittingly said, neither do you enter, nor do you permit those entering to enter, especially if we see them, by their evil life and pride and revilings and avarice, leading into scandal not, I will say, one of the little ones, but even, as far as lies in them, all. Woe, then, to those who shut the kingdom of heaven before men, either in this way or in another; but blessed are those who open it either by their word or by their good work, like him who said: "a great and evident door has been opened to me", or as the rest of the apostles opened it. And if anyone becomes an imitator of them, he opens the kingdom of heaven before men by his justice and virtue and chastity and wisdom. And the more one advances in piety, the more he opens the kingdom of heaven before men.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: I think, therefore, that all who profess that they enter into the church, altogether either shut the kingdom of heaven before men by their evil manners of life insofar as they themselves sin, or open it by their good acts insofar as they have conducted themselves justly. Most of all do this those who seem to be more illustrious in the church, such as bishops, presbyters, deacons.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For by living well and teaching well the word of truth they open the kingdom of heaven before men and, while they themselves enter, they provoke others to enter; but the evil ones, who are not shepherds but hirelings, shut the kingdom of heaven before men and do not hear what the Apostle says: "but we endure all things, that we may give no offense to the Gospel of Christ".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Indeed one may see many teachers not permitting to enter into the kingdom of heaven those who desire to enter — especially when, without judgment and without reason, not on account of the sins which they commit, they excommunicate certain persons, but on account of some jealousy and contentiousness they frequently forbid to enter even those who are better than they themselves are. And they indeed are not permitted to enter, but those others, who are sober in mind and watchful in spirit, overcoming by their patience and long-suffering the tyrannies of these men, though forbidden nevertheless enter and inherit the kingdom of heaven.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Next let us see whether, beyond those we have spoken of, it is possible to see also others who shut and open the kingdom of heaven. For those who have been counted worthy and fit to expound the Gospel, and who show themselves such that they can truly say "Do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?", open the kingdom of heaven before men, when they demonstrate, with all clarity and proof, the loftiness of the divine words — words which were not spoken about earthly things but about heaven and about the mind of the Lord, who came to men — so that, so far as it lies in them, they would lead "Gentiles and barbarians, wise and unwise" to the piety of Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But those who, through their unteachableness and unrighteousness, with much rashness gave themselves over to the profession of teaching before they had learned and come to know the truth, and who therefore, in imitation of vain Jewish fables, hand down the bodily narratives of the Scriptures and not their spiritual sense or intention, and who moreover disparage those "who have risen with Christ and seek the things that are above" in the Scriptures "and not upon the earth," nor reckon that the truth set forth in the Scriptures lies in earthly things: these, so far as it lies in them, shut the kingdom of heaven before men, shutting it by their unrighteousness and drawing to themselves those who were able — by hearing the more divine and greater teaching and the loftiness of the truth — to enter into the kingdom of heaven through the heavenly doctrines and through the deeds befitting them. To this exposition it is fitting what Luke writes: "Woe to you lawyers, for you have taken away the key of knowledge;
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: you yourselves have not entered in, and you have hindered those who were entering." For those who accuse the allegorical exposition and want to teach that the divine Scripture is plain and has nothing more than the text shows, and who do not admit any more divine sense concerning circumcision or the Passover or the unleavened bread or foods and drinks or the feasts or the new moons or the sabbaths, and do not accept that the Jews then served "in the display and shadow of things to come" — these indeed are lawyers, yet they have taken away "the key of knowledge," so far as their teaching goes, that is, taking away every way of the law for understanding its ordinances;
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: and therefore neither did they themselves enter in nor, so far as it lay in them, did they permit others to enter.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: By the kingdom of heaven is meant the Scriptures, because in them the kingdom of heaven is lodged; the understanding of these is the door. Or the kingdom of heaven is the blessedness of heaven, and the door thereof Christ, by Whom men enter in. The door-keepers are the Priests, to whom is committed the word of teaching or interpreting Scripture, by which the door of truth is opened to men. The opening of this door is right interpretation. And observe that He said not, Woe unto you, for ye open, but, for ye shut up; the Scriptures then are not shut up, though they are obscure.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Which means that every one who thinks highly of his own deserts, shall be humbled before God; and every one who humbles himself concerning his good deeds, shall be exalted with God.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: Or, because their observance of the kingdom of heaven proceeds hence, that they may keep up their practice of going about to widows' houses, they shall therefore receive the heavier judgment, as having their own sin and the ignorance of others to answer for.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: These are the poisoners of truth. They are reluctant to undertake the salvation of others. They bolt shut the kingdom of heaven. In their ambition they "devour widows' houses and for pretense make long prayers." By this acquaintance with heaven (achieved with those long prayers), they expect they will persevere in the merits of grace quietly, just as a rich person expects to receive the treasure stored up for him. However, they will receive ample judgment and punishment for their particular sins. They will be called to account for their strange and ignorant practices.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: "Woe unto you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows' houses, and for a pretense make long prayers: therefore ye shall receive greater damnation."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: After this, next He derides them for gluttony: and the grievous thing was, that not from rich men's goods, but from the poor they indulged their own belly, and aggravated their poverty, which they should have relieved. For neither did they merely eat, but devoured.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: Moreover also the manner of their overreaching was yet more grievous, "for a pretense making long prayers."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: For every one is worthy of vengeance who doeth any evil thing; but he that is deriving even the reason for so doing from godliness, and is using this cloke for his wickedness, is justly liable to a far more grievous punishment. And wherefore did He not depose them? Because the time suffered it not as yet. So therefore He lets them alone for a time, but by His sayings, He secures that the people be not deceived, lest, through the dignity of those men, they be drawn on to the same emulation.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: For as He had said, "Whatsoever they bid you do, that do;" He shows how many things they do amiss, lest from thence He should be supposed amongst the unwise to commit all to them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: The Pharisees and the Scribes then would neither enter in, nor hear Him who said, By me if any man enter in he shall be saved; (John 10:9.) nor would they suffer those to enter in, who were able to have believed through the things which had been spoken before by the Law and the Prophets concerning Christ, but shut up the door with every kind of device to deter men from entering. Also they detracted from His teaching, denied all prophecy concerning Him, and blasphemed every miracle as deceitful, or wrought by the Devil.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: All who in their evil conversation set an example of sinning to the people, and who commit injustice, offending the weak, seem to shut up the kingdom of heaven before men. And this sin is found among the people, and chiefly among the doctors, when they teach men what the Gospel righteousness requires of them, but do not what they teach.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But those who both teach and live well open to men the kingdom of heaven, and both enter in themselves, and invite others to enter in. Many also will not suffer those who are willing to enter into the kingdom of heaven, when they without reason excommunicate out of jealousy others who are better than themselves; thus they refuse them entrance, but these of sober spirit, overcoming by their patience this tyranny, although forbidden, yet enter in and inherit the kingdom.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Also they who with much rashness have set themselves to the profession of teaching before they have learned, and following Jewish fables, detract from those who search out the higher things of Scripture; these do, as far as in them lies, shut out men from the kingdom of heaven.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The female sex is imprudent, as not contemplating with reason all that it sees or hears; and weak, as being easily turned either from bad to good, or from good to bad. The male sex is more prudent and hardy. And therefore pretenders to holiness practise most upon women, who are unable to see their hypocrisy, and are easily inclined to love them on the ground of religion. But widows they chiefly choose to attempt; first, because a woman who has her husband to advise her is not so readily deceived; and secondly, she has not the means of giving, being in the power of her husband. The Lord then, whilst He confounds the Jewish Priests, instructs the Christian that they should not frequent widows rather than others, for though their purpose may not be bad, it gives occasion to suspicions.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: First, for that ye are wicked, and then because ye put on the cloak of sanctity. Your covetousness you dress up in the colour of religion, and use God's arms in the Devil's service, that iniquity may be loved while it is thought to be piety.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (cont. Faust. xvi. 29. et cf. cont. Adimant. 16.) This He said not because proselytes were circumcised, but because they imitated the lives of those from following whom He had prohibited His disciples, saying, Do ye not after their works. Two things are observable in this command; first, the honour shown to Moses' teaching, (Matt. 23:3.) that even wicked men when sitting in his seat are compelled to teach good things; and that the proselyte is made a child of hell, not by hearing the words of the Law, but by following their doings. And twofold more than they for this reason, that he neglects to fulfil what he had undertaken of his own choice, having been not born a Jew, but of free will become a Jew.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: (Mor. xxxi. 9.) But forasmuch as hypocrites though they do ever crooked things, yet cease not to speak right things, and thus by their good instructions beget sons, but are not able to bring them up by good life, but the more they give themselves up to worldly works, the more willingly do they suffer those whom they have begotten to work the same. And because their hearts are hardened, these very sons whom they have begotten they do not own by any sign of the affection due. Wherefore it is here said of the hypocrites, And when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: That they compass sea and land signifies that throughout the whole world they shall be enemies of Christ's Gospel, and shall bring men under the yoke of the Law against the justification of faith. There were proselytes made into the Synagogue from among the Gentiles, the small number of whom is here denoted by what is said one proselyte. For after the preaching of Christ there was no faith left in their doctrine, but whoever was gained to the faith of the Jews became a child of hell.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: And he becomes the child of a twofold punishment, because he has not obtained remission of his Gentile sins, and because he has joined the society of those who persecuted Christ.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: Or otherwise; The Scribes and Pharisees compassed the whole world to make proselytes of the Gentiles, that is, to mix the uncircumcised stranger with the people of God.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Or, because before while he was a Gentile he erred in ignorance, and was only a child of hell; but seeing the vices of his masters, and understanding that they destroyed in their actions what they taught in words, he returns to his vomit, and becoming a Gentile, he is worthy of greater punishment as one that has deserted his cause.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: He is called a child of hell in the same way as one is said to be a child of perdition, and a child of this world; every man is called the son of him whose works he does.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Verse 15.) Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you travel over sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as yourselves.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: We do not serve with the same zeal with which we seek. Scribes and Pharisees, while traversing the whole world for the sake of gains or different profits to be sought both by attracting disciples and by the image of holiness, they had the intention to make a proselyte, that is, a stranger and uncircumcised, mix with the people of God. But he, who before, while he was an ethnick, simply wandered, and was once the son of Gehenna, seeing the vices of the masters, and understanding to destroy them by works, what they were teaching by words, returns to his vomit: and becoming a gentile, as if a transgressor, he will be worthy of a greater punishment. But he is called the son of Gehenna, just as the son of perdition, and the son of this age. For each one is called the son of him whose works he does.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: After this, again another charge: "Ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves;" that is, not even the fact that hardly ye have taken him, and with endless toils, induces you to be sparing towards him, although of the things we have hardly acquired, we are more sparing, but you not even this renders more gentle.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: Here He lays to their charge two things; one, that they are unprofitable for the salvation of the many, and need much toil in order to win over even one; another, that they were remiss in the preservation of him whom they had gained, or rather that they were not only careless, but even traitors, by their wickedness in their life corrupting him, and making him worse. For when the disciple sees his teachers to be such as these, he becomes worse than they. For he stops not at his teacher's wickedness; but as when his teacher is virtuous, he imitates him, so when he is bad, he even goes beyond him, by reason of our proneness to what is evil.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: And He calls him "a child of hell," that is, a very hell. And He said "twofold more than you," that He might both alarm those, and make these feel the more severely, because they are teachers of wickedness. And not this only, but because they labor to instill into their disciples a greater wickedness, hardening them to a much greater depravity than they have, and this is above all a mark of a depraved soul.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: From this place we learn that there will be a difference of torment in hell, seeing one is here said to be singly a child of hell, another twofold. And we ought to consider here whether it is possible that a man should be generally a child of hell, as a Jew, suppose, or a Gentile, or whether specially so in consequence of some particular sins; that as a righteous man is increased in glory by the abundance of his righteousnesses, so a sinner's punishment is increased manifold by the number of his sins.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who go about the sea and the dry land to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him a son of gehenna twice as much as you yourselves are.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: These things are fittingly said, after the coming of Christ, to the scribes and Pharisees of Jewish words, who diligently go about very many places of the world in order to persuade newcomers to Judaize. For whoever Judaize after the Savior are taught to imitate the disposition of those who said at that time: "Crucify, crucify him", and again "Away with such a one from the earth"; and they are taught also to accuse him, just as then the priests of the people used to accuse him. And it is possible to see them even now, when a robber is being judged and a Christian bears witness to the truth, wishing rather that the imitator of Barabbas be acquitted than the disciple of Christ. All of which things make the proselyte a son of gehenna not simply, but, as it is written, twofold beyond the scribes and Pharisees who made him a proselyte.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But someone will say in this place: how is the disciple, a proselyte to those who are now the wretchedly constituted scribes and Pharisees, not made a son of gehenna equally with his teachers, but twofold? For he will say that he ought to become a son of gehenna less, and, if anything, by half, than the one who made him a proselyte. Or, if one should even grant that the disciple be "as his master", the disciple ought to become a son of gehenna equally with his master. I think, therefore, that every man who from the Gentile manner of life has been made a proselyte of the Jews was a son of gehenna even before he becomes a proselyte.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For a life subjected to idolatries is sufficient of itself to make a man a son of gehenna. Such a son of gehenna, therefore, the word of our Lord Jesus Christ does indeed save and set free through the "washing of baptism", giving him the power to become a son of God and showing him the way, so that he may become a son of God the Father who is in heaven. But the word of the Jews who do not believe in Christ not only does not release the Gentile from gehenna, but still adds to him a further count of damnation, so that according to Judaism too he becomes a son of gehenna.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And thus the scribe or Pharisee makes another a son of gehenna more than himself, not because he himself makes him twofold, but because, when the man has been made …, he is made twofold a son of gehenna through the teaching of his teacher. And thus the one who taught becomes the cause of that man's second error, so that he becomes twofold a son of gehenna above the one who taught him ill. But another will say in another way, that those who from the beginning were nurtured in the law of Moses are already sons of gehenna, because they did not believe in Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But those who have left the Gentile life, once judging to abandon the idolatry in which they had been nurtured, and have taken hold of the Jewish life, are worthy of a double punishment, because they did not abandon it with inquiry, nor were they willing to examine the Jewish word and that which seems to be akin to the Jewish word, that is, the profession of Christians, nor did they investigate through those who are competent to teach both sects, so that they might understand which word was the truer and rather to be chosen.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: At the same time we learn from this place that among those also who are to be in gehenna there will be a difference of torments, since the one is simply a son of gehenna, while the other is twofold.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But this too we must consider: whether someone becomes a son of gehenna still more abundantly, for instance threefold or manifold according to the multitude of his sins; and whether it is generally the case that someone becomes a son of gehenna, for instance a Jew or a Gentile or the professor of any false doctrine whatsoever, or also specially, so that through the individual kinds of sins one becomes a son of gehenna: for instance, he who fornicates becomes a son of gehenna, but he who also commits adultery becomes so twofold, while he who also commits theft becomes so still threefold (according to what is written: "with what measure you have measured, with the same measure it shall be measured to you"), so that the righteous man indeed is increased in glory according to the number of his righteous deeds, but the sinner is multiplied in gehenna according to the number of his sins. But what this gehenna is, and in what place of the scriptures it was first named, let him who is able inquire, especially in the division of the inheritance of Joshua the son of Nun, where sometimes it is called the valley of the son of Hinnom, but sometimes the valley of Hinnom, which is Gehenna (for Ge is a VALLEY), and let him observe that, just as Jerusalem is the portion of the tribe of Benjamin and certain other chosen cities or villages, so also is Gehenna.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And it is consequent for him who knows what Jerusalem is in the division of the true inheritance of the sons of Israel, that he should understand the discourse about gehenna. But he who reads Joshua the son of Nun diligently, let him see also which villages are there reported to neighbor the valley that is called Gehenna. It has seemed to me not to be safe to hand these things down at greater length and more openly through ink and pen and paper; would that these very things which we do say may not seem to have been said rashly and perilously!
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And that not of compassion from desire to save him whom they taught, but either from covetousness, that the greater number of worshippers might increase the number of offerings made in sacrifice, or out of vain glory. For he who sinks himself in a slough of sins, how should he be desirous to rescue another out of them? Will a man be more merciful to another than to himself? By a man's actions therefore it may be known whether he seeks another's conversion for God's sake, or out of vain glory.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Or, because while he was a worshipper of idols, he observed righteousness even because of men; but when he became a Jew, prompted by the example of evil teachers, he became worse than his teachers.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (Quæst. Ev. i. 34.) The temple and altar we may also understand of Christ Himself; the gold and the gifts, of the praise and sacrifice of prayer which we offer in Him and through Him. For not He by them, but they by Him, are sanctified.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: For since Christ is come, reliance upon the Law is vain; for not Christ by the Law, but the Law by Christ, is sanctified, in whom it rests as on a seat or throne; so are they fools and blind, who, overlooking the sanctifier, pay honour to the things sanctified.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: As by making broad phylacteries and fringes they sought after the reputation of sanctity, and made this again a means of gain, so now He charges them with being teachers of wickedness by their fraudulent pretence of tradition. For when in any dispute or quarrel, or ambiguous cause, one swore by the temple, and was afterwards convicted of falsehood, he was not held guilty. This is what is meant by that, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing, that is, he owes nothing, But if he had sworn by the gold, or by the money which was offered to the Priests in the temple, he was immediately compelled to pay down that by which he had sworn.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Verse 16 onwards) Woe to you, blind guides, who say, 'Whoever swears by the temple is nothing, but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound by his oath.' Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And, 'Whoever swears by the altar is nothing, but whoever swears by the gift that is on it is obligated.' Blind!
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: For which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift? Therefore, whoever swears on the altar, swears on it and on all things that are above it. And whoever swears in the temple, swears in it and in him who dwells in it. And whoever swears in heaven, swears on the throne of God and on him who sits on it. Above, as it seemed to us, we have explained what the tradition of the Pharisees meant, saying: Whatever gift is from me will benefit you: now the double tradition of the Pharisees, enticing to one occasion of greed, is condemned, so that they may be proved to do everything for gain and not for the fear of God. For just as in the phylacteries and fringes, by enlarged expectations of holiness, it was trying to capture glory, and was seeking gains through the opportunity of glory, so another tradition found fault with the teachers of impiety.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: If anyone were to swear in the temple during a dispute, or in some argument, or in a doubtful case, and later be convicted of lying, they were not held accountable for the crime. But if they were to swear on gold and money, which was offered to the priests in the temple, they were immediately compelled to fulfill what they had sworn. Again: If anyone swore upon the altar, no one held him guilty of perjury; but if he swore falsely on a gift, or on offerings, that is, on victims and on fine flour and on the rest, which are offered to God upon the altar, these were most diligently sought after.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Therefore, the Lord reproached them both for foolishness and deceit, because the temple is much greater than the gold that is sanctified by the temple, and the altar is greater than the offerings that are sanctified by the altar. But they did it not out of fear of God, but out of greed for riches.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Now an oath is in confirmation of somewhat that has been spoken. The oath here then may signify testimony of Scripture which we produce in confirmation of that word which we speak. So that Divine Scripture is the temple of God, the gold is the meaning which it contains. As the gold which is outside the Temple is not sanctified, so all thoughts which are without divine Scripture, however admirable they may seem, are not hallowed. We ought not therefore to bring any speculations of our own for the confirmation of doctrine, unless such as we can show are hallowed by being contained in divine Scripture.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The altar is the human heart, which is the chief thing in man. The offerings and gifts that are hid upon the altar, are every thing which are done in the heart, as to pray, to sing, to do alms, to fast. Every offering of a man then is sanctified by his heart, by which the offering is made. There cannot therefore be a more honourable offering than the heart of man, out of which the offering proceeds. If then one's conscience does not smite him, he has confidence towards God, not by reason of his gifts, but so to speak because he has rightly ordered the altar of his heart. Thirdly, we may say that over the temple, that is over every Scripture, and over the altar, that is over every heart, there is a certain meaning which is called the Heaven, the throne of God Himself, in which we shall be able to see the things that are revealed face to face, when that which is perfect is come.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Woe to you, guides of the blind, who say: whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, is bound. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And: whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it, is bound. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift? He therefore who swears by the altar swears by it and by all things that are upon it. And he who swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. And he who swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: By this saying too he censures the traditions of the Pharisees, as being not upright. He does this also in that passage where he reproaches the traditions of the Pharisees made against the commandment of God, which had been laid down concerning the honor of father or mother, when the Pharisees said: "whoever shall say to his father or mother: a gift, whatever from me may profit you, he shall not honor his father".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: After which he adds and says: "you have made void the commandment of God, that you may establish your own tradition", and he brings forward the example of Isaiah, saying: "this people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; and in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men". One, then, of the Pharisaic traditions was such, concerning those who swear, since some indeed swore by the temple, but others by the gold of the temple, likewise others by the altar, others by the gift of the altar; and they said that he was a debtor who swore by the gold of the temple or by the gift of the altar, but that he was in no respect liable who swore by the temple or by the altar.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore, speaking against traditions of this kind to the Jews, and wishing to correct them from human traditions to the divine commandments, the Savior says that they are blind and foolish who hand down such things, not seeing that everything which is placed in the temple is not sanctified through itself, but through the temple. So too what is placed upon the altar is judged to be already God's gift from the fact that it has been received upon the altar.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: If, then, the cause of sanctifying the gold is the temple, and of sanctifying the gift the altar, how would it not seem foolish that the one who swears by that which sanctifies is not guilty, while the one who swears by that which is sanctified seems to be guilty, as though that which is sanctified were better than that which sanctifies?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: So, since the Jews have the custom of swearing also by heaven, to the foregoing he added this too for the reproof of those who swore more readily by heaven than by God, since he acts equally irrationally who swears by heaven, just as he who swears by the temple or by the altar; for he who swears by heaven is seen also to swear by him who sits upon it, and does not (as he supposes) escape the danger from the fact that he swears not by God himself, but by the throne of God. And these things he says to the Jews, forbidding men to give heed to the traditions of the Pharisees. For otherwise, above, he plainly forbade to swear "at all".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if it is necessary to bring somewhat more deeply to light, at least in part, the meaning of Scripture that lies hidden as it were in such fields of the Gospel and is not comprehensible to just anyone, it must be said: every oath is a binding and a confirmation of the word about which one swears.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore an oath is to be understood as every testimony of the Scriptures that is brought forward for the confirmation and binding of our word which we speak, so that "all Scripture divinely inspired" is indeed the temple of the glory of God, and the meaning placed within it is the gold. Therefore, in support of all the words that we bring forward in teaching, we ought to bring forward the meaning of Scripture as though confirming the meaning that we set forth. For just as all gold that is outside the temple is not sanctified, so every meaning that is outside the divine Scripture (however admirable it may seem to some) is not holy, because it is not contained by the meaning of Scripture, which is accustomed to sanctify only that meaning which it has within itself, as the temple sanctifies its own proper gold. We ought not, therefore, in order to confirm our teaching, to swear by our own private understandings and take them as testimonies, those things which each one of us understands and reckons to be according to truth, unless he has shown them to be holy, from the fact that they are contained in the divine Scriptures as though in certain temples of God. Fools therefore and blind are all those who do not recognize that the temple, that is, the reading of the Scriptures, makes a meaning great and venerable, as it does the consecrated gold.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But consider further whether perhaps, according to the likeness of the temple and the gold placed in the temple, we ought to understand the altar and the gift which is placed upon the altar. The altar, then, which sanctifies the offering, is the heart of man, which is held to be the principal thing in man; and the offerings and gifts which are placed upon the altar are everything that is placed upon the heart.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For instance, you propose to pray: you have placed the offering of prayer upon your heart, as upon a certain altar, in order to offer prayer to God. You have proposed to sing psalms: you have placed the offering of psalms upon your heart, as upon a certain altar, in order to offer to God the offering of psalms.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: You have proposed to give alms: you have placed the offering of almsgiving upon your heart, as upon a certain altar, in order to offer the offering of almsgiving to God. You have proposed to fast: you have placed the offering of fasting upon your heart, as upon a certain altar …. Therefore the heart of man, from which the offering is offered to God, makes every offering venerable and holy. For this reason the offering cannot be more honorable than the heart of man, from which the offering is transmitted.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Blind, therefore, is every man who sees either someone's great almsgivings or psalms or great prayers or fastings, and without judgment pronounces them blessed, and does not consider from what sort of heart the almsgivings are offered, or the psalms, or the prayers, or the fastings. For the altar is the heart which sanctifies the offering of him who is pure of heart. For if the heart and conscience of a man "does not prick him, he has confidence toward God". Not on account of his gifts, nor the words of prayer or psalm, however well composed they may seem and selected from the Scriptures, but because (so to speak) he has well built the altar of his heart. He, therefore, who takes the altar, that is, the principal heart and the conscience, as witness, swears by the altar, embracing everything that is contained in it. And he who swears, according to what we have handed down, by the temple, that is by Scripture, is seen to swear by Scripture and by the word and meaning of God which is contained in it.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But there is a third point, that we may say that above the temple, that is, above all Scripture, and above the altar, that is, above every heart, there is a certain understanding above the understanding of all the Scriptures and above every heart, "which has not yet ascended into the heart of man", which morally is called heaven, a throne now not "of the glory of God", as the temple is, but of God himself. For the temple is the temple of the glory of God, in which "we see through a mirror in an enigma"; but heaven, which is above the temple of God himself, in which is the throne of God, in which it is possible to behold "with unveiled face", "when that which is perfect shall have come", the face of the mysteries of the truth that sit in a heaven of this kind.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The temple pertains to God's glory, and to man's spiritual salvation, but the gold of the temple though it pertains to the glory of God, yet does it more so to the delight of man, and the profit of the Priests. The Jews then pronounced the gold which delighted them, and the gifts which fed them, to be more holy than the temple, that they might make men more disposed to offer gifts, than to pour out prayers in the temple. Whence the Lord suitably reproves them in these words. Yet have some Christians at present an equally foolish notion. See, they say, in any suit if one swear by God, it seems nought; but if one swear by the Gospel, he seems to have done some great thing. To whom we shall say in like manner, Ye fools and blind! the Scriptures were written because of God, God is not because of the Scriptures. Greater therefore is God, than what is hallowed by Him.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Jesus is saying that the gold in the temple, the gold objects dedicated in the temple to the glory of God, whether these be the gold cherubim or the gold jar containing the manna, were considered by the Jews to be worthy of much more honor than the temple. Therefore they were condemned by the Lord.… But the saying possesses a figurative meaning directed against them because they are not receiving the truth regarding Christ. Instead, they were judging Moses and the types given through him as more valuable than Christ.… They were rejecting the Christ who sanctifies Moses while simultaneously praising the law. Just as the law was praiseworthy, not because it possesses the types and the symbols but because it prefigures the true mystery of worship in Christ, in the same way the gold is precious because of the one who sanctifies the temple, and heaven is beautiful because of the God who sanctifies it and dwells within it.
paragraphs.author: Theodore of Heraclea

paragraphs.text: For since Christ is come, reliance upon the Law is vain; for not Christ by the Law, but the Law by Christ, is sanctified, in whom it rests as on a seat or throne; so are they fools and blind, who, overlooking the sanctifier, pay honour to the things sanctified.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: Again, if one swore by the altar, none held him guilty of perjury; but if he swore by the gift or the victims or the other things which are offered to God upon the altar, this they exacted most rigorously. And all this they did not out of fear of God, but out of covetousness. Thus the Lord charges them with both folly and fraud, inasmuch as the altar is much greater than the victims which are sanctified by the altar.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: For since Christ is come, reliance upon the Law is vain; for not Christ by the Law, but the Law by Christ, is sanctified, in whom it rests as on a seat or throne; so are they fools and blind, who, overlooking the sanctifier, pay honour to the things sanctified.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: His hands, at all events, are ever unclean, eternally dyed with the blood of the prophets, and of the Lord Himself; and on that account, as being hereditary culprits from their privity to their fathers' crimes, they do not dare even to raise them unto the Lord, for fear some Isaiah should cry out, for fear Christ should utterly shudder.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: In like manner the custom which the Jews had of swearing by the Heaven He reprobates. For they did not, as they supposed, avoid the danger of taking an oath by God, because, Whose sweareth by heaven, sweareth by the throne of God, and by him that sitteth thereon.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "O Pharisees, you demand," Jesus says, "perhaps the tithes of herbs and the smallest coins while you neglect the commandments, concerning which the violation is greater." And what kind of commandments are these? Justice, that is, to judge uprightly and blamelessly; mercy, that is, genuineness toward God. For justice and mercy and faith toward God are better than the tithe and firstfruits. Therefore the God of all things says through the prophet, "And now, Israel, what does the Lord require from you but to do justice and to love and seek mercy and to be prepared to follow the Lord your God." For the genuine faith of those being saved is seen in their exceeding readiness to follow.
paragraphs.author: Cyril of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: A hermit was asked by a brother, 'How do I find God? With fasts, or labour, or vigils, or works of mercy?' He replied, 'You will find Him in all those, and also in discretion. I tell you many have been very stern with their bodies, but have gained nothing by it because they did it without discretion. Even if our mouths stink from fasting, and we have learnt all the Scriptures, and memorized the whole Psalter, we may still lack what God wants, humility and love.'
paragraphs.author: Desert Fathers
paragraphs.work: The Desert Fathers, Sayings of the Early Christian Monks

paragraphs.text: (Mor. i. 15.) Or otherwise; The gnat stings while it hums; the camel bows its back to receive its load. The Jews then strained off the gnat, when they prayed to have the seditious robber released to them; and they swallowed the camel, when they sought with shouts the death of Him who had voluntarily taken on Him the burden of our mortality.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: And because it was much less guilt to omit the tithing of herbs than a duty of benevolence, the Lord derides them, Ye blind guides, which strain out a gnat, and swallow a camel.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: God laughs at the superficial diligence of those who measure cucumbers. God laughs at our attempts to swallow camels, as if the sins of avoidance were less serious than the sins of consumption.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: What is lost is the hidden dimension of the evil will. These hidden things of the mind bring about these distortions of the law. The law prescribes that a tenth be given, so they measure out a tenth of a measure of mint and dill but only in order that they might be thought by other men to fulfill the law. They abandon mercy and justice, faith and every form of benevolence. Yet these are the true duties of man.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: The Lord had commanded, that for the maintenance of the Priests and Levites, whose portion was the Lord, tithes of every thing should be offered in the temple. Accordingly, the Pharisees (to dismiss mystical expositions) concerned themselves about this alone, that these trifling things should be paid in, but lightly esteemed other things which were weighty. He charges them then with covetousness in exacting carefully the tithes of worthless herbs, while they neglected justice in their transactions of business, mercy to the poor, and faith toward God, which are weighty things.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: The camel I suppose to mean the weighty precepts, judgment, mercy, and faith; the gnat, the tithing of mint, anise, and cummin, and other valueless herbs. The greater of God's commands we swallow and overlook, but show our carelessness by a religious scrupulousness in little things which bring profit with them.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Verse 23.) Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. Many precepts are given in the law that foreshadow future events. But others are open, according to the Psalmist, saying: The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes (Psalms 19:8), which are immediately to be desired.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: For example, thou shalt not commit adultery: thou shalt not steal: thou shalt not bear false witness, etc. But the Pharisees, because the Lord had commanded (let us for the present leave out the mystical understanding) tithes to be offered in the temple for the maintenance of the priests and Levites, whose portion was the Lord's, were studious in this one thing, that the commands should be observed: but as to the other matters, whether a man should do them or not, they made little account.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And from this chapter it accuses them of greed, because they eagerly demand tithes even of cheap vegetables, and neglect justice in the handling of business disputes, and mercy towards the poor, orphans, and widows, and faith in God, which are great.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Then He derides them for folly also, because they bade them disregard the greater commandments. And yet before He had said the opposite, that "they bind heavy burdens, and grievous to be borne." But these things too they did again and were doing everything for the corruption of those who were subject to them, in little things requiring strictness, and despising the great.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: "For ye pay tithe," He saith, "of mint and anise, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, and mercy, and faith. These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the others undone."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: Here then He naturally saith it, where it is tithe and almsgiving, for what doth it hurt to give alms? But not to keep the law; for neither doth it say thus. Therefore here indeed He saith, "These ought ye to have done;" but where He is speaking about clean and unclean, He no longer adds this, but makes a distinction, and shows that the inward purity is necessarily followed by the outward, but the converse is no longer so.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: For where there is a plea of love to man, He passes it over lightly, for this very reason, and because it was not yet time expressly and plainly to revoke the things of the law. But where it is an observance of bodily purification, He overthrows it more plainly.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: Then, to show that there is no harm arising from despising bodily cleansings, but very great vengeance from not regarding the purifications of the soul, which is virtue, He called these "a gnat," for they are small and nothing, but those other a camel, for they were beyond what men could bear. Wherefore also He saith, "Straining at the gnat, and swallowing the camel." For indeed the one were enacted for the sake of the other, I mean of mercy and judgment; so that not even then did they profit being done alone. For whereas the little things were mentioned for the sake of the great, and after that these last were neglected, and labor was spent on those alone, nothing was gained even then by this. For the greater followed not the lesser, but the lesser were sure to follow these greater.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: But these things He saith to show, that even before grace was come, these were not among the principal things, or amongst those upon which men should spend their labor, but the matters required were different. But if before the grace they were so, much more when high commandments had come, were these things unprofitable, and it was not meet to practise them at all.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: In every case then is vice a grievous thing, but especially when it does not so much as think it needs amendment; and it is yet more grievous, when it thinks itself sufficient even to amend others; to express which Christ calls them "blind guides." For if for a blind man not to think he needs a guide be extreme misery and wretchedness; when he wishes himself to guide others, see to what a gulf it leads.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: But these things He said, by all intimating their mad desire of glory, and their exceeding frenzy concerning this pest. For this became a cause to them of all their evils, namely, that they did all things for display. This both led them away from the faith, and caused them to neglect what really is virtue, and induced them to busy themselves about bodily purifyings only, neglecting the purifications of the soul. So therefore to lead them into what really is virtue, and to the purifyings of the soul, He makes mention of mercy, and judgment, and faith.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: For these are the things that comprise our life, these are what purify the soul, justice, love to man, truth; the one inclining us to pardon and not suffering us to be excessively severe and unforgiving to them that sin (for then shall we gain doubly, both becoming kind to man, and hence meeting also ourselves with much kindness from the God of all), and causing us both to sympathize with them that are despitefully entreated, and to assist them; the other not suffering them to be deceitful, and crafty.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: But neither when He saith, "These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the others undone," doth He say it as introducing a legal observance; away with the thought; neither with regard to the platter and the cup, when He said, "Cleanse that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also," doth He bring us unto the old regard for little things, but on the contrary indeed, He doth all things to show it to be superfluous. For He said not, Cleanse the outside of them also, but that which is within, and the outside is sure to follow.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and you have left behind the weightier things of the law, judgment and mercy and faith; but these things it was necessary to do, and not to omit those. Blind guides, straining out a gnat, but swallowing a camel (23, 23. 24).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: This word must be spoken at a fitting time to those who indeed display religion toward God in the smallest matters, but in matters great and necessary hold in contempt the commandment and God himself who commanded them. Such things happened even among the Jews, who supposed themselves to be keeping the law of Moses, who prescribed that from all fruits tithes be given to the Levites and the priests.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And so, since it was easy to fulfill the law in the smallest matters, they tithed indeed mint and dill and cumin, and all (so to speak) the smallest things and those that were light in the law, but its weighty things they did not observe, that is, judgment and mercy and faith: judgment indeed, that each one should judge concerning all things with a just judgment and not concerning only some, and should assent to him who said: "I desire mercy, rather than sacrifice", so that he might offer to God the sacrifices of acts of mercy, so that, examining those things which are of faith, he might be faithful.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But since it was fitting that certain of those hearing the Lord speak these things about tithing the smallest matters might come to despise the tithing of the smallest things, the Lord wisely added, saying: and these it was necessary to do (that is, judgment and mercy and faith) and not to omit those (that is, the tithing of mint and dill and cumin). And he says that those who do such things, the scribes and Pharisees, who omit the weightier things of the law and tithe the contemptible things among the fruits, are blind guides.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And he wisely says that such men strain out (that is, expel from themselves) the smallest faults, which he named gnats, but "swallow" (that is, commit) the greatest faults, which he named camels, animals evidently twisted and huge. According to these words, therefore, every man who omits the weightier things of the law (especially judgment and mercy and faith) swallows a camel. And not only among the Jews, but also among us, one may find many sinning sins of this kind and swallowing camels, in that they commit the greatest faults; and one may frequently observe men of this kind, how in the smallest matters they display their religion.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And he rightly calls them hypocrites; for wishing to acquire religiosity "before men", they are unwilling to take up that religiosity which God has justified. We must therefore flee such pretenses of the scribes and Pharisees, lest that woe befall us also, just as it befell them.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But I judge that, morally, all are called scribes who suppose nothing more to be set down in the Scriptures than what the plain wording of the Scripture shows, but who moreover despise those who "search out the depth of God". Likewise all are Pharisees who justify themselves and separate themselves from the rest, "saying: Do not draw near to me, for I am clean". Now the Pharisees are interpreted, according to the name Phares, as THE DIVIDED, who divided themselves from the rest; for Phares in the Hebrew tongue means DIVISION.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if in words of the Gospel of this kind one must also take up a moral understanding, it must be known that, just as mint and dill and cumin are seasonings of foods and not themselves the principal foods, so in our ways of life there are certain things that are indeed principal and necessary for the justification of our souls — such as these weightier matters of the law, judgment and mercy and faith — but others that are, as it were, seasonings of our acts, commending them and making them more pleasant, such as abstaining from laughter and fasting, the bending of the knees, perseverance in the assemblies, assiduity in the communion, and other things like these, which are not themselves the justices, but are held to be the seasonings of the justices.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the spiritual things that are justices of themselves are called judgment and mercy and faith. It is disgraceful, therefore, to observe these least things (which is to tithe), yet not to offer to God the observances of the necessary things (that is, not to tithe). And those who do and teach these things, like the former ones, are blind guides. And how should they not be reckoned blind, from whom the greatness and the twistedness of camels — that is, of perverse acts — lies hidden, and who do not see that it profits nothing to strain out and to be scrupulous as an examiner in the least matters, while the principal things and those that truly pertain to the glory of God are neglected?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Since, therefore, there are many even among us who suppose they are living carefully with regard to trivial matters, but with regard to the necessary matters despise themselves, the present discourse confounds men of this sort — not indeed forbidding them to observe those trivial things, but commanding them to guard more carefully the principal and more salutary things.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He, therefore, strains out all things who, in all things whatsoever he does or speaks or thinks, separates what is sordid and earthly and not adorned with divine reasonings from those things that are by nature bright and sincere and just, according to him who teaches: "let us keep the feast not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But you will find many who are reckoned to believe, yet do not have their words and acts and thoughts strained out. Therefore "as hay" shall "the fire consume" their carnal acts, torturing the soul also together with the body on account of the bodily faults grown fast to it. For just as it is not possible to cut away the superfluities grown upon bodies without great pain and torment for those who suffer them, so neither the carnal deeds from those who (so to speak) have made their souls flesh; wherefore it was said concerning such souls: "my spirit shall not remain in these men, for they are flesh".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But because it was possible that some, hearing the Lord speak thus, might thereupon neglect paying tithes of small things, He prudently adds, These things ought ye to have done, (i. e. justice, mercy, and faith,) and not to leave the others undone, i. e. the tithing of mint, anise, and cummin.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now this is the first lust which conquered the world, and because of it the first transgression of the law took place. Through it the scribes and Pharisees received "Woe" from our Redeemer, because it had taught them to keep festival, and Sabbath, and to pay tithe of cummin. For the lust of the belly is the captain of the host of the left side, and to it are fettered all the hosts of sin.
paragraphs.author: Philoxenus of Mabbug

paragraphs.text: Or, because these covetous Priests, when any one did not bring his tithes of the smallest thing, made it a matter of grave reprehension; but when one injured his neighbour or sinned against God, they were at no pains to reprove him, careful only of their own profit, neglecting the glory of God, and the salvation of men. For to observe righteousness, to do mercy, and to have faith, these things God commanded for His own glory; but the payment of tithes He established for the support of the Priests, so that the Priests should minister to the people in spiritual things, and the people supply the Priests with carnal things.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Thus is it at this time, when all are careful of their own honour, none of God's honour; they jealously protect their own rights, but will not bestow any pains in the service of the Church. If the people pay not their tithes duly, they murmur; but if they see the people in sin, they utter not a word against them. But because some of the Scribes and Pharisees, to whom He is now speaking, were of the people, it is not unsuitable to make a different interpretation; and 'to tithe' may be used as well of him who pays, as of him who receives, tithes.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: The Scribes then and Pharisees offered tithes of the very best things for the purpose of displaying their righteousness; but in their judgments they were unjust, without mercy for their brethren, without faith for the truth.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: In these words the Lord shows that all the commandments of the Law, greatest and least, are to be fulfilled. They also are refuted who give alms of the fruits of the earth, supposing that thus they cannot sin, whereas their alms profit them nothing unless they are careful to keep themselves from sin.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: (Verse 24) Blind leaders, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel. I believe the camel refers to the understanding of the present situation, the magnitude of the teachings, judgment, mercy, and faith. The gnat, on the other hand, represents the tithing of mint, dill, cumin, and other cheap herbs. We devour and neglect these great commandments of God, while showing diligence in matters of religion that bring profit and have little importance.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Or, straining out a gnat, that is, putting from them small sins; swallowing a camel, that is, committing great sins, which He calls camels, from the size and distorted shape of that animal.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Morally, The Scribes are those who think nothing else contained in Scripture than the bare letter exhibits; the Pharisees are all those who esteem themselves righteous, and separate themselves from others, saying, 'Come not nigh me, for I am clean.' Mint, anise, and cummin, are the seasoning, not the substantial part of food; as in our life and conversation there are some things necessary to justification, as judgment, mercy, and faith; and others which are like the seasoning of our actions, giving them a flavour and sweetness, as abstinence from laughter, fasting, bending the knee, and such like. How shall they not be judged blind who see not that it is of little avail to be a careful dispenser in the least things, if things of chief moment are neglected?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: These His present discourse overthrows; not forbidding to observe the little things, but bidding to keep more carefully the chief things.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The law of Moses taught through the use of symbols how to maintain purity throughout life's activities. It was the custom of the Jews, passed on to them from their ancient traditions, to wash carefully their cups and the dish that contained their food. They observed these practices to maintain their purity and to avoid contact with "sinful people." Their aim was that they might flee from fellowship with sinners.… How much more through such practices were they preparing themselves to flee from sin itself.
paragraphs.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

paragraphs.text: And yet those who were carefully observing these practices were themselves acting like robbers and violently making a profit, becoming loathsome by doing so. Therefore Jesus says this: "Flee unrighteousness, O blind Pharisee. For you fail to perceive how you are acting. For what is in the cup and dish are clean if they are not gained in an unrighteous manner. Righteousness cleanses the vessel much better than water."
paragraphs.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

paragraphs.text: (Mor. i. 15.) Or otherwise; The gnat stings while it hums; the camel bows its back to receive its load. The Jews then strained off the gnat, when they prayed to have the seditious robber released to them; and they swallowed the camel, when they sought with shouts the death of Him who had voluntarily taken on Him the burden of our mortality.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: He therefore is reproving those who, pursuing an ostentation of useless scrupulosity, neglected the discharge of useful morality. For it is the inside of the cup that is used; if that be foul, what profit is it to cleanse the outside? And therefore what is needed is purity of the inner conscience, that those things which are of the body may be clean without.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: In different words, but to the same purport as before, He reproves the hypocrisy and dissimulation of the Pharisees, that they showed one face to men abroad, but wore another at home. He means not here, that their scrupulousness respecting the cup and the platter was of any importance, but that they affected it to pass off their sanctity upon men; which is clear from His adding, but inwardly ye are full of ravening and uncleanness.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Verse 25, 26.) Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and impurity. Blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and the plate, so that the outside also may be clean. In different words, with the same meaning as above, Jesus accuses the Pharisees of hypocrisy and deceit, because they pretend one thing to others outwardly, but do something different at home. Not that their superstition delayed them in the cup and dish; but that they displayed holiness to others, in their attire, in their speech, in their phylacteries, in the fringes, in the length of their prayers, and other such things, while internally they were full of the filth of vices.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: So, therefore, while with respect to alms He saith, "These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the others undone," touching purifications He speaks not on this wise, but what? "Ye make clean," He saith, "the outside of the cup and the platter, but within they are full of extortion, and injustice. Cleanse that which is within the cup, that the outside may be clean also." And He took it from a thing confessed and manifest, from a cup and platter.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: And besides, neither is it concerning a cup and platter he is speaking, but of soul and body, by the outside meaning the body, by the inside the soul. But if with regard to the platter there be need of that which is within much more with regard to thee.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: But ye do the contrary, saith He, observing things trifling and external, ye neglect what are great and inward: whence very great mischief arises, for that thinking ye have duly performed all, ye despise the other things; and despising them, ye do not so much as strive or attempt to perform them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

paragraphs.text: This discourse instructs us that we should hasten to become righteous, not to seem so. For whoso seeks to be thought so, cleanses the outside, and has care of the things that are seen, but neglects the heart and conscience. But he who seeks to cleanse that which is within, that is, the thoughts, makes by that means the things without clean also. All professors of false doctrine are cups cleansed on the outside, because of that show of religion which they affect, but within they are full of extortion and guile, hurrying men into error.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The cup is a vessel for liquids, the platter for meat. Every discourse then of which we spiritually drink, and all speech by which we are fed, are vessels for meat and drink. They who study to set forth well wrought discourse rather than such as is full of healthful meaning, are cups cleansed without; but within full of the defilement of vanity. Also the letter of the Law and the Prophets is a cup of spiritual drink, and a platter of necessary food. The Scribes and Pharisees seek to make plain the outward sense; Christ's disciples labour to exhibit the spiritual sense.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean what is outside of the cup and the dish, but within you are full of plunder and intemperance and deceit. Blind Pharisee, clean first what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may become clean (23, 25, 26).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: This saying instructs us to be eager to be just, not to appear just. For whoever is intent on appearing just cleans the things that are outside and attends to what is seen, but neglects his own heart and conscience — not considering that the one who is intent on the things that are within and is eager to clean his own thoughts, consequently is also eager to make clean the things that are outside. But if anyone is eager for the things that are seen and yet neglects the interior things of his soul, it is necessary that such a man be filled from within with avarice, wantonness, malice, and very many other evils.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For everyone who is anxious about his own salvation (which is from within) is also anxious about his reputation (which is from outside); but not everyone who is anxious about his reputation from outside is also anxious about his own salvation from within.
