For it is by the blessing of God that we retain the memory of God. Also the memory of God is slain by the wicked, when the Temple of God is polluted by the lustful, and His altar defiled by the carelessness of prayers. Abel is interpreted 'mourning.' He then who does not receive that, Blessed are they that mourn, sheds the blood of Abel, that is, puts away the truth of wholesome mourning. Some also shed, as it were, the blood of the Scriptures by putting aside their truth, for all Scripture, if it is not understood according to its truth, is dead.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: As all the good things which had been merited by all the saints in each generation since the foundation of the world were bestowed upon that last generation which received Christ; so all the evil that all the wicked in every generation from the foundation of the world had deserved to suffer, came upon that last generation of the Jews which rejected Christ.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Or thus; Assail the righteous of former saints, yea, of all the saints, could not merit that so great grace as was given to men in Christ; so the sins of all the wicked could not deserve so much evil as came upon the Jews, that they should suffer such things as these suffered from the Romans, and that in after time every generation of them to the end of the world should be cast off from God, and be made a mock by all the Gentiles. For what is there worse than to reject and in such sort to put to death the Son coming in mercy and lowliness!
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Or thus; Nations and states when they sin are not thereupon immediately punished by God, but He waits for many generations; but when He sees fit to destroy that state or nation, He then seems to visit upon them the sins of all former generations, and one generation suffers the accumulation of all that former generations have deserved. Thus this generation of the Jews seems to have been punished for their fathers; but in truth they suffered not for others, but on their own account.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: That is, all the vengeance due for the shedding of the blood of the righteous.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: It should be enquired too how He says, to the blood of Zacharias, since the blood of many more saints was afterwards shed. This is thus explained. Abel a keeper of sheep was killed in the field, Zacharias a priest was slain in the court of the temple. The Lord therefore names these two, because by these all holy martyrs are denoted, both of lay and priestly order.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: Otherwise; Because He delayed the punishment of hell which He had threatened them with, He pronounces against them threats of present evil, saying, All these things shall come upon this generation.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: For he who having seen many sinning yet remains uncorrected, but rather does the same or worse, is obnoxious to heavier punishment.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: He was soon to rain calamitous blows on Jerusalem because of its bloodthirsty nature. For that very reason Jesus accuses it of possessing a murderous disposition. For he says it kills the prophets and stones the ones sent to it. So often [the city] could have obtained mercy, but it does not desire it. How many times he demonstrated this, on many occasions and to many descendants, as when he brought back the people from captivity. But through their sins they continually scattered themselves. By speaking of wings and shelter Jesus teaches in a way appropriate for God and illustrates the meaning of Moses' words through a human comparison.
paragraphs.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

paragraphs.text: "He spread his wings and welcomed them." And David: "But the children of men take refuge in the shadow of your wings." For when Satan scattered them on one side into idolatry and on the other into a love for pleasure, he sent prophets to them. Then through himself he came that he might gather them together "into one." But they could not bear to remain under his protection. "For I," he says, "like a loving hen always held you to draw you to myself, but you had no desire for this. You scattered yourself through your constant sinning and drew away from God." But this is a prolific hen who has many children. She ardently loves and cares for her children and willingly gives herself for them.
paragraphs.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

paragraphs.text: (Quaest. Ev. i. 36.) This species has the greatest affection for its brood, insomuch that when they are sick the mother sickens also; and what you will hardly find in any other animal, it will fight against the kite, protecting its young with its wings. In like manner our mother, the Wisdom of God, sickened as it were in the putting on the flesh, according to that of the Apostle, The weakness of God is stronger than men, (1 Cor. 1:25.) protects our weakness, and resists the Devil that he should not make us his prey.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: (Ench. 97.) Where is that omnipotence, by the which He did whatsoever pleased Him both in heaven and in earth, if He would have gathered the children of Jerusalem and did not? Was it not that she would not that her children should be gathered by Him, and yet He did, notwithstanding, gather those of her children whom He would?
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: Admonition, then, is the censure of loving care and produces understanding. Such is Christ the Educator in his admonitions, as when he says in the Gospel, "How often would I have gathered your children, as a bird gathers her young ones under her wings, and you would not!" And again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, "And they committed adultery with wood and stone and burned incense to Baal." For it is a very great proof of his love, that, though knowing well the shamelessness of the people that had kicked and bounded away, he notwithstanding exhorts them to repentance and says by Ezekiel, "Son of man, you live among scorpions.
paragraphs.author: Clement of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, speak to them. Perhaps they will hear." Further, to Moses he says, "Go and tell Pharaoh to send my people forth; but I know that he will not send them forth." For he shows both things: both his divinity in his foreknowledge of what would take place and his love in affording an opportunity for repentance to the self-determination of the soul. He admonishes also by Isaiah, in his care for the people, when he says, "This people honor me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." What follows is reproving censure: "In vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of people." Here his loving care, having shown their sin, shows salvation side by side with repentance.
paragraphs.author: Clement of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: the Lord Christ, who in those days when he had come down from the Mount of Olives, and beheld Jerusalem and wept over it as it lay opposite, said: How often would I have gathered thy children even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wing, and ye would not. Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: (Verse 37.) Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you: how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling! Jerusalem, He calls not the stones and buildings of the city, but the inhabitants, whom He mourns for with a fatherly affection, as we also read in another place that He wept upon seeing her (Luke 19). And in saying, how often I have longed to gather your children together, He testifies that all the prophets sent by Himself were rejected. We also read in the song of Deuteronomy the image of a chicken gathering its chicks under its wings: As an eagle protects its nest and desires its young, spreading its wings, it receives and carries them on its feathers (Deut. XXXII, 11).
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: By Jerusalem He means not the stones and buildings, but the dwellers there, over whom He laments with the feeling of a Father.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Then He directs His speech unto the city, in this way too being minded to correct His hearers, and saith, "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem!" What meaneth the repetition? this is the manner of one pitying her, and bemoaning her, and greatly loving her. For, like as unto a woman beloved, herself indeed ever loved, but who had despised Him that loved her, and therefore on the point of being punished, He pleads, being now about to inflict the punishment. Which He doth in the prophets also, using these words, "I said, Turn thou unto me, and she returned not."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: Then having called her, He tells also her blood-stained deeds, "Thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not," in this way also pleading for His own dealings; not even with these things hast thou turned me aside, nor withdrawn me from my great affection toward thee, but it was my desire even so, not once or twice, but often to draw thee unto me. "For how often would I have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens, and ye would not." And this He saith, to show that they were ever scattering themselves by their sins. And His affection He indicates by the similitude; for indeed the creature is warm in its love towards its brood. And everywhere in the prophets is this same image of the wings, and in the song of Moses and in the Psalms, indicating His great protection and care.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets, and stone those who are sent to you, how often have I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not? behold, now your house shall be left to you desolate. For I say to you, that from now on you shall not see me until you say: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: It is worth inquiring how the Savior, speaking before hearers among whom were scribes and Pharisees who prided themselves on knowing carefully the things of the law and the prophets, on what ground he said that Jerusalem had killed the prophets and had stoned those sent to her, since no such account is much prophesied in the ancient scriptures that were read in their synagogues. We do read that Jeremiah was cast into a pit of mud, yet not that he was killed in Jerusalem. But neither of Isaiah nor of Ezekiel nor of any of the prophets do we read that he suffered any such thing, so far as my memory suggests.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But searching in the second book of Chronicles, where many things are written about the famous prophets, I find that Asa, angered at Hanani the prophet who rebuked him, did indeed put him in prison, yet did nothing more to him. And Ahab too ordered Micaiah, who prophesied against him, to go into the prison house and to eat the bread of tribulation, yet did not kill him. But we read of one who was stoned, "Azariah the son of Jehoiada the priest," who was rebuking the people. Therefore we do not find, beyond what I have said, that in Jerusalem prophets were killed, or that those sent to Jerusalem were stoned.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For this reason it must be considered whether perhaps it is necessary to demonstrate the word of Christ from the more secret books which are current among the Jews — and not only the word of Christ but also of his disciples, of Stephen the first martyr and of Paul the apostle. For Stephen speaks thus: "O stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so also you. For which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And they killed those who announced the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now become the betrayers and murderers"; and after this: "they drove him outside the city, and they stoned Stephen crying out and saying." And Paul, in the first letter to the Thessalonians, says such things concerning the killing of the prophets: "you became imitators of the churches of God which are in Judea in Christ Jesus, since you too suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews, who both killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and persecuted us, and do not please God." And to the Hebrews thus: "they were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were tempted, they died by the sword, they went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being in want, distressed, afflicted with sufferings — of whom the world was not worthy — wandering in deserts and in mountains and caves and holes of the earth." It is reported, then, in the scriptures that are not manifest, that Isaiah was sawn in two, and Zechariah killed, and Ezekiel.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And I suppose that Elijah, who wandered in the desert and in the mountains, is the one who went about in sheepskins and goatskins. But suppose someone rejects the letter to the Hebrews as not being Paul's, and likewise casts away the secret book of Isaiah: yet what will he do with the words of Stephen, or of Paul to the Thessalonians, brought forward about the prophets killed, or with those of our Lord himself? Or how will he reject that which Paul brought forward to Timothy, saying: "as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth"? For we do not know in the canonical books the account of Jannes and Jambres resisting Moses.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if he also looks at what is set down in the first letter to the Corinthians, "what eye has not seen nor ear heard," can anyone possibly reject all these things?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: All these things we have said in examining the passage, not being ignorant that many of the secret writings have been fabricated by the impious and by those who speak "iniquity on high." And the followers of Hypythianus use certain fabricated writings, and others those of Basilides. It is necessary, therefore, to consider carefully, so that we neither accept all the secret writings that are circulated in the name of the saints — on account of the Jews, who perhaps have fabricated certain things to the destruction of the truth of our scriptures, establishing false doctrines — nor reject all that pertain to the demonstration of our scriptures.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: It belongs, then, to a great man to hear and fulfill what has been said: "test all things, hold fast what is good." Yet on account of those who cannot, like money-changers, discern among words whether they are to be held true or false, and who cannot keep themselves carefully, so as to hold what is true with them but "abstain from every evil appearance," no one ought to use, for the confirmation of doctrines, books that are outside the canonical scriptures.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, if anyone accepts the letter to the Hebrews as Paul's, he will say that we ought not refer plurals altogether to many. For not many were sawn in two, but Isaiah alone; nor were many stoned except Azariah only, the son of Jehoiada; nor was anyone killed by the sword except Zechariah the son of Barachiah; so too in sheepskins and in goatskin, Elijah, and other like cases.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And further let us inquire into what is written in Luke, the Lord saying: "because it cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem." If, then, "it cannot be that a prophet perish outside Jerusalem," that is, be killed, you will ask whether after the destruction of Jerusalem there is now no prophet, lest perhaps the one who is killed "outside Jerusalem" should, being a prophet, prove the word of Christ false. But if the scriptures compel us — on account of Agabus and the daughters of Philip the evangelist (not on account of the false prophets of Phrygia) — let us inquire whether perhaps every righteous person is in Jerusalem and not "outside Jerusalem," since "it cannot be" that the one who is outside Jerusalem be afflicted with sufferings for the sake of the word.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But how Jerusalem killed the prophets must be considered. And I judge that, as people are accustomed to say in common speech — the city cried out, as if it were said, those who are in the city; likewise, the city went out to meet him, that is, those who are in the city — so: Jerusalem killed the prophets, that is, those who were in Jerusalem, on whose account it was said that Jerusalem killed the prophets. And if the citizens are put for the city, again a question arises: who are to be called the children of Jerusalem, concerning whom it was said: how often have I wished to gather your children?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But we say that the successors of the citizens are always called the children of those who preceded them. But that Jerusalem which is free from the servitude of sin, which is above in its manner of life, "which is our mother," does not kill the prophets nor stone those who are sent to her. It is another matter that, after the likeness of that Jerusalem which killed and stoned the prophets, frequently there are certain persons set up in this Jerusalem, unskilled and not fearing God, who (as far as in them lies) kill and stone, with words uttered without judgment, men advanced in word and in life — men who indeed do not abandon the canon of the churches, but on account of the profundity of their doctrines are held suspect by those who are accustomed to say certain novel things and do not attend to the "sound word" of our Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The Lord, therefore, says to Jerusalem the killer and stoner of the prophets: how often have I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not? How is it that here the Lord Jesus, as one who often wished to gather the Jews but did not gather them on account of the obstinacy of those unwilling to believe, says thus: how often have I wished, when it is plain that he taught the Jews in the body only once? But not only in his presence, but also substantially, Christ was always present both in Moses and in the prophets, and still more in the angels ministering to human salvation through the individual generations; and thus is fulfilled what he says: how often have I wished.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For through the individual generations he always wished and hastened to accomplish the will of the Father in them, and though not established in the body, as now at the end of the ages, yet he always hastened to gather the children of Jerusalem.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the very words of him wishing to gather the children of Jerusalem are found in the law and in the prophets, and of him it is written: "spreading out his wings he received them, and took them up upon his shoulders"; and it is the daily work of Christ to gather the children of Jerusalem (concerning whom many things are said both in Isaiah and in the rest of the prophets), and daily the Son of God gathers the scattered children of God, as a hen her chicks under her wings.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if anyone has not been gathered by him, he will be judged as one who was unwilling to be gathered by him. "For the Son of Man came to seek what had perished, and to save," and he died "not for the nation alone, but that he might gather into one the scattered children of God." And to the Jews indeed (who were the children of that Jerusalem which was below) he threatened, as they were unwilling to be gathered under his wings, saying: behold, now your house shall be left to you desolate.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And always to those who are unwilling to be gathered under his wings Christ seems to threaten and to say: behold, now your house shall be left to you desolate, that is, your soul and body. For not only the body, but also the soul of those who sin, is left desolate, and (as in a desert) foxes make lairs in them, and serpents, the brood of vipers, their resting-places.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But he says to those unwilling to be gathered to him: that you shall not see me from now on until you say: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. And not even then did the Jews see Christ, for he was not seen by them rising from the dead as before, but by judgment and grace only by the fathers who were worthy. And until, understanding their own desolation, they say in penitence: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, they will not see the Son of God, nor will they see his word, nor will they consider the beauty of the wisdom of God. But even if any of us should wish to be gathered under the wings of Christ, yet by evil works should refuse to be gathered under his wings, he will now not see the word of God — especially from that time from which he flees the one who gathers him, day by day, by his action rather than by his body. And so long he will not see the beauty of the word, that is, Christ himself, until, converted and repentant from his evil purpose, he says: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. For then the blessed word of God and the blessed wisdom of God, coming, comes in the name of God and of the Father upon the heart of man, when someone has been converted to him.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He calls them children of Jerusalem, just as we call each generation of citizens the sons of the preceding generation. And He says, How often, though it is well known that once only did He teach the Jews in the body, because Christ was ever present in Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Angels, ministering to human salvation in every generation. Whosoever shall not have been gathered in by Him shall be judged, as though he had refused to be gathered in.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Foreseeing the destruction of the city, and the blow it would receive from the Romans, He called to mind the blood of the saints which had been, and should yet be, shed in it. Thou killedst Esaias who was sent unto thee, and stonedst my servant Jeremias; thou dashedst out the brains of Ezechiel by dragging him over stones; how shalt thou be saved, which wilt not suffer a physician to come nigh thee? And He said not, Didst kill and stone; but, Killest, and Stonest; that is, This is a common and natural practice with thee to kill and stone the saints. She did to the Apostles the same things which she had once done to the Prophets.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (non occ.) Let heretics then cease to assign to Christ a beginning from the Virgin; let them leave off to preach one God of the Law and another of the Prophets.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: Verse 38. Behold, your house shall be left desolate. This very thing Jeremiah had already said in the person of Jeremiah: I have forsaken my house, I have cast off my inheritance: my inheritance is become to me as a lion in the forest. We see with our eyes the house of the Jews left desolate, that is, that temple which shone more brightly, because it lost its inhabitant Christ, and, desiring to seize the inheritance, killed the heir.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "But ye would not," He saith. "Behold your house is left desolate," stripped of the succor which cometh from me. Surely it was the same, who also was before protecting them, and holding them together, and preserving them; surely it was He who was ever chastening them. And He appoints a punishment, which they had ever dreaded exceedingly; for it declared the entire overthrow of their polity.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: In like manner to all such as would not be gathered under His wings Christ speaks this threat; Behold, your house is left unto you desolate; i. e. your soul and your body. But if any one of you will not be gathered under the wings of Christ, from the very time when he shall have refused to be so gathered, (by a mental rather than a bodily act,) he shall no more see the beauty of the word, till repenting of his evil purpose he shall say, Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord. And the word of the Lord then comes with a blessing upon a man's heart, when one is turned to God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: As the body, when the spirit departs, first becomes cold, and then decays and decomposes; so also your temple, when God's Spirit shall have withdrawn, shall be first filled with strife and anarchy, and after shall come to ruin.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: That which has been spoken possesses an interpretation that comes through the vision of faith. For when "the fullness of the nations come in" and they believe in Christ, then the Jews who believe after these things see the beauty of the divine nature of Christ. They behold the Father in the Son and declare him to be the Redeemer proclaimed through the prophets, whom the prophets previously mentioned as coming in the name of the Lord. For the other prophets did not come in the name of the Lord. For they were saying, "The Lord says these things" and "I am the servant of the Lord, and I worship the God of heaven."
paragraphs.author: Cyril of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (Verse 39) For I tell you, you will not see me again until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.' He is speaking to Jerusalem and to the people of Judaea. However, this verse, in which even infants and nursing babies used at the entrance of the Lord's Savior in Jerusalem, when they said, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, hosanna in the highest,' is taken from the 117th psalm, which clearly is written about the coming of the Lord. And what he says, he wants this to be understood: Unless you repent (Luke 13), and confess that I am the one about whom the Prophets sang, the Son of the almighty Father, you will not see my face. The Jews have been given a time of repentance: let them confess the blessed one who comes in the name of the Lord, and let them contemplate the face of Christ.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: I say unto you, Ye shall not see Me, &c. That is to say, Unless ye shall do penitence, and shall confess that I am He of whom the Prophets have spoken, the Son of the Almighty Father, ye shall not see My face. Thus the Jews have a time allowed for their repentance. Let them confess Him blessed who cometh in the name of the Lord, and they shall then behold Christ's face.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord." And this is the language of one that loves earnestly, earnestly drawing them unto Him by the things to come, not merely warning them by the past; for of the future day of His second coming doth He here speak.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: What then? Did they not see Him from that time? But it is not that hour which He meaneth in saying, Henceforth, but the time up to His crucifixion.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: For since they were forever accusing Him of this, that He was a kind of rival God, and a foe to God, He moves them to love Him by this, namely, by showing Himself to be of one accord with His Father; and He indicates Himself to be the same that was in the prophets. Wherefore also He uses the same words as did the prophets.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: And by these He intimated both His resurrection, and His second coming, and made it plain even to the utterly unbelieving, that then most surely they should worship Him. And how did He make this plain? By speaking of many things that were first to be, that He should send prophets, that they should kill them; that it should be in the synagogues; that they should suffer the utmost extremities; that their house should be left desolate; that they should undergo things more grievous than any, and such as never were undergone before. For all these things are enough to furnish even to the most senseless and contentious a clear proof of that which should come to pass at His coming.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: For I will ask them, Did He send the prophets and wise men? Did they slay them in their synagogue? Was their house left desolate? Did all the vengeance come upon that generation? It is quite plain that it was so, and no man gainsays it. As then all these things came to pass, so shall those also come to pass, and most surely they shall submit then.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74

paragraphs.text: But they shall derive thence no advantage in the way of defense, as neither will they who repent of their course of life then.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 74
